name: LLM Application Engineering
level: In-depth engineering course · no official exam
audience: Software engineers and architects building production LLM features, RAG systems and agents, alone or in small teams.
format: This site's course with a 40-question practice test of design, debugging, evaluation and cost questions across providers.

domains.name: Model APIs, prompting and structured output
domains.summary: How the Anthropic, OpenAI and Google text APIs differ in system prompts, conversation state and stop reasons, plus prompting that holds up on current models, schema-constrained structured output with validation and repair, token budgeting and context rot, and routing across model tiers and providers.

domains.name: Retrieval and RAG
domains.summary: Building retrieval that finds the right evidence: ingestion and chunking, embeddings and their versioning, HNSW, BM25 and hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion, reranking and contextual retrieval, and measuring it all with recall@k, MRR and nDCG on a labelled set.

domains.name: Tools, agents and MCP
domains.summary: The tool-use loop and its failure modes, workflow patterns versus autonomous agents, designing tools agents use well, the stateless 2026-07-28 Model Context Protocol, and context engineering for long-running agents with memory, compaction and sub-agents.

domains.name: Evaluation
domains.summary: Treating evals as regression tests for prompt and model changes: building eval sets from real traffic, programmatic checks, LLM judges and their biases, the statistics needed to compare two systems honestly, and running evals in CI and production.

domains.name: Production: cost, latency and reliability
domains.summary: Running LLM features in production: per-feature cost models with cached and batch pricing, latency levers such as streaming and prompt caching, retries, timeouts and fallbacks, OpenTelemetry GenAI tracing, and gradual rollout of model and prompt versions.

domains.name: Security, safety and privacy
domains.summary: Why prompt injection cannot be filtered away and which architectures contain it, the OWASP Top 10 for LLM applications (2025), agent permissions and exfiltration channels, PII and retention including zero data retention limits, and content-safety guardrails.

scenarios.title: Shipping a support assistant with RAG
scenarios.description: Answer customer questions from a help centre and ticket history. Chunk and index the content, combine vector and keyword search, cite the passages used, keep each tenant's documents separate, and measure retrieval before tuning prompts.

scenarios.title: Building an agent with tools and MCP
scenarios.description: Give a model a small set of well-described tools, some served over MCP. Handle tool errors and turn limits, keep tool output small, require approval for risky actions, and manage context as the task runs long.

scenarios.title: Cutting LLM cost and latency in half
scenarios.description: Model cost per feature from input, output and cached tokens. Then apply prompt caching, batch jobs, smaller models for easy routes and streaming, and check that quality holds on the eval set.

scenarios.title: Setting up evals before a model upgrade
scenarios.description: Build an eval set from real traffic, pick programmatic checks and calibrated LLM judges, compare the old and new model with confidence intervals, and gate the switch in CI with a gradual rollout.

scenarios.title: Defending an app against prompt injection
scenarios.description: An assistant reads email, web pages and documents it does not control. Limit what injected text can do through privilege separation, least-privilege tools, closed exfiltration channels and human approval, rather than relying on filters.

lessons.title: Messages APIs across providers
lessons.summary: Anthropic Messages, OpenAI Responses and Google Interactions all turn a list of turns into a typed response, but they differ in where the system prompt goes, who owns conversation state, and how they tell you why generation stopped.

sections.heading: Three request shapes
sections.body:
Every major provider now has one primary text-generation endpoint:

| | Anthropic Messages | OpenAI Responses | Google Interactions |
|---|---|---|---|
| Call | `client.messages.create(...)` | `client.responses.create(model, input)` | `client.interactions.create(model, input)` |
| System-level guidance | top-level `system` field | top-level `instructions` (or a `developer`-role message) | `system_instruction` |
| Read the text | iterate `content` blocks | `response.output_text` | `interaction.output_text` |
| Required | `model`, `max_tokens`, `messages` | `model`, `input` | `model`, `input` |

OpenAI still supports Chat Completions, but recommends Responses for new projects. Google describes Interactions as its default interface as of June 2026, with `generateContent` kept as legacy.

**Read typed output, not positions.** A Responses `output` is an array of typed items (reasoning, messages, tool calls). Code that reads `output[0]` breaks as soon as a reasoning item or tool call comes first. Use `output_text` or iterate by type. The same applies to Claude `content` blocks.

sections.heading: Roles and the system prompt
sections.body:
Roles carry authority. On OpenAI the order is `developer` above `user`, and `assistant` holds model output. On Claude the system prompt is a separate top-level field, not a message in the list, and `messages` alternate `user` and `assistant`.

Put durable rules (persona, policies, output contract) in the system or developer slot and the task-specific request in the user turn. Do not paste untrusted content into the system prompt: it inherits the highest authority.

sections.heading: Who owns multi-turn state
sections.body:
- **Anthropic Messages is stateless.** You resend the full history each call. Your application decides what to keep, trim or summarize. (A server-side message-threads feature is in beta; check its data-retention terms before using it.)
- **OpenAI Responses stores responses by default** (30 days). Set `store: false` when you must not keep data on the provider side.
- **Google Interactions chains turns** with `previous_interaction_id`, but `tools`, `system_instruction` and `generation_config` are interaction-scoped: re-send them on every turn or the next turn runs without them.

A provider abstraction must make these differences explicit rather than pretend every API behaves like one of them.

sections.heading: Stop reasons are control flow
sections.body:
On Claude, `stop_reason` tells you why generation ended. Branch on it; never infer completion from the text.

- `end_turn`: natural finish.
- `max_tokens`: hit your output cap. The output is truncated.
- `stop_sequence`: one of your stop sequences was generated.
- `tool_use`: run the requested tools and send `tool_result` blocks back.
- `pause_turn`: a server-tool loop hit its iteration limit. Send the content back unchanged to continue.
- `refusal`: the model declined. It is an **HTTP 200**, and `stop_details` is populated only for this reason. Consider retrying on a fallback model.
- `model_context_window_exceeded`: the context filled up. Treat as truncated.

An `end_turn` with only 2 to 3 tokens is usually caused by putting a text block right after `tool_result` blocks. Fix the message shape; do not retry the same request unchanged. OpenAI reports refusals as a `refusal` content part and truncation as `status: "incomplete"`.

sections.heading: Streaming
sections.body:
Streaming cuts time-to-first-token for chat UIs. On Claude the event order is `message_start`, then content-block start/delta/stop events, then `message_delta`, then `message_stop`.

```python
with client.messages.stream(model=MODEL, max_tokens=1024,
                            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Hello"}]) as stream:
    for text in stream.text_stream:
        print(text, end="", flush=True)
```

Two traps: `stop_reason` is null in `message_start` and arrives in `message_delta`; and an error event (for example `overloaded_error`) can arrive mid-stream after the HTTP 200, so a 200 status does not mean the answer is complete. Usage in `message_delta` is cumulative, so do not add the deltas together.

keyPoints: Anthropic Messages is stateless; you resend history. OpenAI Responses stores responses by default unless store is false.
Gemini Interactions chains with previous_interaction_id but tools and system_instruction must be re-sent every turn.
Read typed output (output_text, content blocks by type), never a fixed array index.
Branch on stop_reason: refusal is HTTP 200, max_tokens and model_context_window_exceeded mean truncated.
In a Claude stream, stop_reason arrives in message_delta, and errors can arrive after the HTTP 200.

gotchas.trap: A refusal is an HTTP error, so the SDK retry logic covers it.
gotchas.correct: A Claude refusal is an HTTP 200 with stop_reason "refusal". Branch on it explicitly.

gotchas.trap: Read the answer from output[0] of a Responses call.
gotchas.correct: output is an array of typed items. Use output_text or iterate by item type.

gotchas.trap: With previous_interaction_id, the tools from turn 1 carry over.
gotchas.correct: Tools, system_instruction and generation_config are interaction-scoped. Re-send them each turn.

lessons.lab: Write one function `generate(provider, system, history, user)` that calls Anthropic Messages and OpenAI Responses and returns `{text, stopped_because, truncated, refused}`. Force truncation with a tiny `max_tokens` / `max_output_tokens` and confirm both adapters set `truncated`. Then stream the Claude call and log the event types in order, checking where `stop_reason` first becomes non-null.

lessons.title: Prompt engineering that holds up
lessons.summary: Durable prompts are clear about the task and the reason for it, show diverse examples, separate sections with tags, put long material before the question, and let the model's built-in thinking do the reasoning. Several older tricks (prefill, temperature, manual thinking budgets) no longer work on current models.

sections.heading: Clear instructions with the why
sections.body:
Write the prompt as if briefing a capable new colleague with no context. State the task, the audience, the output format and the constraints, and explain **why** each constraint matters. A model that knows "this is read aloud by a screen reader, so no Markdown" generalizes better than one told only "never use Markdown".

Treat prompts as application code: keep them in version control, review changes, and run evals in CI when a prompt changes (OpenAI's prompting guide says the same).

sections.heading: Examples and XML sections
sections.body:
- **Few-shot examples** are the most reliable way to fix format and tone. Anthropic recommends 3 to 5 examples, **diverse** enough that the model does not copy an incidental detail, wrapped in `<example>` tags. Google's guidance is to always include few-shot examples.
- **Delimit sections** with XML tags such as `<instructions>`, `<context>`, `<document>` and `<examples>`, and refer to them by name ("using the contract in `<document>`…"). Consistent delimiters stop the model confusing your instructions with the data.

sections.heading: Long material first, question last
sections.body: For long inputs, put the documents at the top and the question or instructions at the end. Anthropic reports this can improve response quality by up to 30 percent on complex multi-document inputs, and Google gives the same advice (context first, question last). Wrap each document in its own tag with metadata such as source and date.

sections.heading: Prefill and sampling are gone
sections.body:
Two classic tricks are obsolete on current models:

- **Prefill.** Ending the request with a partial assistant turn (for example `{` to force JSON) returns a 400 on current Claude models and on Gemini 3 and later. Use structured outputs for format, and instructions or examples for style.
- **Temperature / top_p / top_k.** The current Claude API version rejects them with a 400 on any model, and recent Gemini models ignore them. Get consistency from structured outputs (enums, schemas), from clear examples, and from evals that run each case several times. Never answer a consistency problem with "lower the temperature" on current models.

sections.heading: Chain of thought and extended thinking
sections.body:
Current reasoning models think before answering, so you control **how much**, not whether:

- **Claude:** adaptive thinking with `output_config.effort` (`low` to `max`). On the newest models thinking is always on, and the old manual `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens}` is not accepted.
- **OpenAI:** `reasoning.effort`, with the allowed values set per model. Reasoning tokens are billed as output.
- **Gemini:** `thinking_level`. Thinking tokens are billed as output and count against `max_output_tokens`.

Manual chain of thought ("think step by step in `<thinking>` tags") is a fallback for when thinking is off. On current Claude models, asking the model to write out its reasoning in tags can trigger a `reasoning_extraction` refusal. Prefer the built-in thinking, and raise or lower effort to trade quality against latency and cost.

keyPoints: Explain the why behind each instruction; the model generalizes from reasons.
Use 3 to 5 diverse examples in <example> tags, and XML tags to separate instructions from data.
Put long documents first and the question last.
Prefill returns 400 on current Claude and Gemini 3+; sampling parameters are rejected or ignored.
Control reasoning with effort / thinking level, not manual chain-of-thought tags.
Version prompts like code and gate changes with evals.

gotchas.trap: Prefill "{" to force JSON output.
gotchas.correct: Prefill is a 400 on current Claude and Gemini 3+. Use the provider's structured-output feature.

gotchas.trap: Set temperature 0 to make labels consistent.
gotchas.correct: Current models reject or ignore sampling parameters. Constrain the output with a schema enum and measure consistency with repeated-trial evals.

gotchas.trap: Ask the model to show its reasoning in <thinking> tags and parse it.
gotchas.correct: Use built-in thinking and effort. Asking for tagged reasoning can trigger a reasoning_extraction refusal.

lessons.lab: Take a 20-case classification task. Run prompt A (bare instruction, question first) and prompt B (instruction with reasons, 3 diverse `<example>` blocks, documents in tags before the question). Run each case 5 times on both prompts and report accuracy and label agreement. Then compare B at two effort levels and record latency and output tokens.

lessons.title: Structured outputs and repair
lessons.summary: Constrained decoding guarantees that output matches a JSON Schema subset, but each provider supports a different subset and none guarantees the values are right. Validate every response with Pydantic and repair by cause: schema errors, refusals and truncation each need a different path.

sections.heading: JSON mode is not structured outputs
sections.body:
**JSON mode** (OpenAI `json_object`) guarantees syntactically valid JSON. It does not guarantee your fields, types or enums. **Structured outputs** constrain decoding to a JSON Schema, so required fields and enum values appear.

- **OpenAI:** `text: {format: {type: "json_schema", strict: true, schema}}`, or in the SDK `client.responses.parse(..., text_format=MyModel)` and read `response.output_parsed`.
- **Anthropic:** `output_config.format = {type: "json_schema", schema}`; the SDK's `client.messages.parse(..., output_format=MyModel)` sends a Pydantic class as `output_config.format` and returns `parsed_output`. Tools can also be marked `strict: true`. The older raw-API `output_format` parameter is deprecated.
- **Gemini:** a JSON response format with a schema on the request.

sections.heading: Each provider supports a different schema subset
sections.body:
| | OpenAI strict | Anthropic | Gemini |
|---|---|---|---|
| Optional fields | every field in `required`; optional = union with `null` | supported | supported |
| `additionalProperties` | must be `false` on every object | only `false` | — |
| Numeric bounds (`minimum`/`maximum`) | — | **not supported** | supported |
| String length (`minLength`/`maxLength`) | — | **not supported** | **silently stripped** |
| Composition | no `allOf`, `not`, `if/then/else` | no recursive schemas or external `$ref` | `anyOf`, `$ref` supported |

OpenAI strict mode also caps nesting depth and property count. Anthropic limits the number of strict tools and union-typed parameters per request and returns a 400 ("Schema is too complex for compilation") for schemas that are too complex. The compiled grammar is cached for 24 hours after last use, and **changing `output_config.format` invalidates the prompt cache**, so keep schemas stable.

The practical rule: keep the schema to the portable core (types, required, enums, nesting) and enforce lengths, ranges and cross-field rules in your own validator.

sections.heading: Validate with Pydantic
sections.body:
Define the contract once as a Pydantic model, send its schema to the provider, and validate every response with `Model.model_validate_json(...)` even when the provider claims a guarantee. Put constraints the provider cannot enforce (string length, numeric range, "end date after start date") in field constraints and validators.

Compare enum values case-insensitively or normalize them: Anthropic notes that enum casing can differ from the schema.

sections.heading: Repair by cause
sections.body:
Structured output can still fail to conform, and the cause decides the fix:

1. **Refusal.** Claude sets `stop_reason: "refusal"`; OpenAI returns a `refusal` content part instead of the schema. Do not parse it and do not retry blindly; route to a fallback model or a human.
2. **Truncation.** `max_tokens` / `model_context_window_exceeded` on Claude, `status: "incomplete"` on OpenAI. The JSON is cut off. Raise the output budget or shrink the task, then retry.
3. **Validation error on otherwise complete output.** Retry once with the validation error message added to the prompt, so the model sees exactly what to fix. Cap retries, then fail loudly or queue for review.

Never fill missing fields with silent defaults: that converts a visible failure into wrong data.

keyPoints: JSON mode = valid JSON; structured outputs = schema-shaped JSON; neither = correct values.
OpenAI strict: all fields required, optional via null union, additionalProperties false everywhere.
Anthropic: no numeric bounds, string lengths, recursive schemas or external $ref; changing the format invalidates the prompt cache.
Gemini silently strips minLength/maxLength and similar keywords: validate in app code.
Repair by cause: refusal, truncation and validation error each take a different branch.

gotchas.trap: Strict mode means the JSON is always valid, so skip validation.
gotchas.correct: Refusals and truncation still produce non-conforming output, and no provider checks semantics. Always validate.

gotchas.trap: Put maxLength in a Gemini schema and trust it.
gotchas.correct: Gemini strips minLength/maxLength silently. Enforce lengths in Pydantic.

gotchas.trap: Make a field optional in OpenAI strict mode by leaving it out of required.
gotchas.correct: List every field in required and give the optional one a null union type.

lessons.lab: Define an `Invoice` Pydantic model with a bounded `total`, a `currency` enum and a `notes` field limited to 200 characters. Send its schema with structured outputs to two providers. Write `extract(text)` that validates, retries once with the error message on `ValidationError`, and returns a typed failure on refusal or truncation. Test it with an adversarial input and a tiny output budget.

lessons.title: Tokens, context windows and context rot
lessons.summary: Context windows are now around a million tokens, but tokens are not words, thinking spends output budget, and models get worse as context grows. Budget deliberately and curate the smallest high-signal context.

sections.heading: Count tokens, do not guess
sections.body:
Token counts depend on the tokenizer, and tokenizers change between model generations. Anthropic states that 1M tokens is roughly 555k words on its current tokenizer, while models before it fit about 750k words in 1M tokens: the same text costs more tokens on the newer models. A rough four characters per token is a planning heuristic, not a budget.

Use the provider's counter for the exact model before you send: Claude has a token-counting endpoint (`/v1/messages/count_tokens`), and every response reports actual `usage`.

sections.heading: Budget the window
sections.body:
A request's window holds system prompt + tools + history + retrieved material + the output. Plan each part:

- **Output budget.** `max_tokens` caps output; hitting it truncates. On Gemini `max_output_tokens` **includes thinking**, so raising the thinking level can starve the visible answer. On OpenAI and Gemini, reasoning or thinking tokens are billed as output.
- **Window size.** Current frontier models list windows around 1M tokens and output caps around 128K, but check the model page; these change.
- **Overflow.** On Claude a full window stops generation with `model_context_window_exceeded`; treat it as truncated.

sections.heading: Context rot and position effects
sections.body:
Bigger windows do not mean free recall. Anthropic describes **context rot**: as the number of tokens grows, the model's ability to recall information from that context decreases, because attention is a finite budget spread across n² pairwise relationships. Liu et al. ("Lost in the Middle") found performance is U-shaped: best when the relevant information is at the start or end of the input, worse in the middle.

So: find the smallest set of high-signal tokens for the task, put key material where the model attends best, and summarize or drop stale turns in long conversations.

sections.heading: Long context or retrieval
sections.body: For a small, stable corpus, the simplest design is often to put all of it in the prompt (with prompt caching for the repeated prefix). Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval post says a knowledge base under 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages) can go straight into the prompt. Above that, or when the corpus changes often, needs per-user permissions, or would dilute attention, retrieve instead (Domain 2).

keyPoints: Tokens are tokenizer-specific; newer tokenizers can use more tokens for the same text. Count with the provider's tool.
The window holds system, tools, history, retrieved context and output.
Thinking or reasoning tokens bill as output, and on Gemini count toward max_output_tokens.
Context rot: recall degrades as context grows; middle positions are recalled worst.
Under about 200K tokens of stable knowledge, putting it all in the prompt can beat building RAG.

gotchas.trap: We have a 1M window, so include every retrieved document.
gotchas.correct: Recall degrades as context grows. Curate the smallest high-signal set.

gotchas.trap: Estimate token cost from word count using last year's ratio.
gotchas.correct: Tokenizers change between generations. Count with the target model's token counter.

lessons.lab: Build a needle test: hide one fact at 10%, 50% and 90% depth in a 100K-token and a 400K-token filler document, and ask for it 5 times each. Plot recall by depth and size. Then count the same document with the token counter for two different model generations and compare.

lessons.title: Model choice, routing and fallbacks
lessons.summary: Pick models by measured quality on your own evals against cost and latency, route easy traffic to cheaper tiers, pin snapshots, and design fallbacks that respect each provider's different failure signals.

sections.heading: Capability, cost and latency tiers
sections.body:
Each provider sells a ladder: a top-capability model, a recommended general model, and small fast models. Per-token prices across the ladder can differ by tens of times (check the pricing page; prices change often). Providers publish a starting point (Anthropic currently suggests its mid-upper Opus tier "for most workloads"; OpenAI suggests its flagship "if you're unsure"), but the real choice comes from your eval set.

Before moving up a tier, try the cheaper lever: Anthropic notes that **tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models**.

sections.heading: Routing
sections.body:
Routing sends each request to the cheapest model that handles it well:

- **Static routing** by task type: a small model for classification and extraction, a larger one for hard reasoning or long documents.
- **Classifier routing:** a small model or a rules layer labels difficulty first.
- **Cascades:** try the cheap model, validate the output, and escalate only failures.

Every route needs its own eval slice, or you will not notice when the cheap path silently degrades.

sections.heading: Pin snapshots and plan upgrades
sections.body: Model IDs on Claude are pinned snapshots, and older models retire on published dates. Pin the exact ID in configuration, keep an eval suite that you rerun before switching, and track deprecation notices. Never hard-code "latest" in production logic.

sections.heading: Fallbacks across models and providers
sections.body:
Distinguish failure types before falling back:

| Signal | What it means | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Claude `stop_reason: "refusal"` (HTTP 200) | model declined | retry on a fallback model or route to review |
| Claude 529 `overloaded_error`; OpenAI 503 `server_is_overloaded` | temporary capacity | back off, then fail over |
| 429 with `retry-after` | rate limited | wait as told |
| Claude 429 with `enforced_spend_limit_reached` and no `retry-after` | spend cap | do not retry; alert and fail over |

A cross-provider fallback is a real port, not a URL swap: the request shape, role names, schema subset, refusal and truncation signals and tokenizer all differ. Validate every provider's output with the same Pydantic model, and run the eval suite on the fallback path too.

keyPoints: Choose by your evals, then cost and latency; try raising effort before switching tiers.
Route easy traffic to cheap tiers; cascade with validation-based escalation.
Pin model snapshot IDs and rerun evals before upgrading.
Separate refusal, overload, rate-limit and spend-cap failures; each has a different action.
Cross-provider fallback needs adapters for shapes, schemas and stop signals, plus its own evals.

gotchas.trap: Use the biggest model everywhere to be safe.
gotchas.correct: Measure smaller tiers on your evals and route; most traffic rarely needs the top tier.

gotchas.trap: Retry every 429 with exponential backoff.
gotchas.correct: A spend-cap 429 has no retry-after and keeps failing. Stop and alert.

lessons.lab: Take a 50-case eval set. Run it on three tiers from one provider and record accuracy, p50 latency and cost per 1,000 requests. Build a cascade (small model first, validate, escalate on failure) and compare its cost and accuracy with the best single model.

lessons.title: RAG Architecture: Ingestion, Chunking and Metadata
lessons.summary: How a retrieval-augmented system is put together, how to chunk and tag documents so retrieval works, and when RAG is the right choice over long context or fine-tuning.

sections.heading: What RAG is
sections.body:
Retrieval-augmented generation pairs a **generator** (the LLM, whose knowledge lives in its weights, its *parametric* memory) with a **retriever** over an external index (*non-parametric* memory). The original RAG paper (Lewis et al., 2020) used a pre-trained neural retriever over a dense vector index of Wikipedia and compared two variants:

- **RAG-Sequence:** the same retrieved passages condition the whole output.
- **RAG-Token:** different passages can be used for each generated token.

Production RAG is usually simpler. You retrieve the top-k chunks once per query, put them in the prompt and ask the model to answer from them, with citations.

sections.heading: The ingestion pipeline
sections.body:
Retrieval quality is mostly decided at ingestion time, long before the query arrives:

1. **Extract** text from the sources (PDF, HTML, tickets). Strip boilerplate, and pull out hidden text so you can review it, because hidden instructions in documents are a known poisoning vector (OWASP LLM08).
2. **Chunk** each document into retrievable units.
3. **Enrich** each chunk with metadata and, optionally, generated context (see Contextual Retrieval in a later lesson).
4. **Embed** each chunk and **index** it, both in a vector index and, for hybrid search, in a lexical (BM25) index.
5. **Record** the embedding model and version, the chunker settings and the source version, so you can re-index reproducibly.

sections.heading: Chunking strategies
sections.body:
There is no universal best chunk size. The trade-off:

- **Small chunks** are precise but lose context. A chunk that says 'revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter' doesn't say which company or which quarter. This is the exact failure Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval post sets out to fix.
- **Large chunks** carry more context but dilute the embedding and use up prompt budget.

Common strategies are fixed-size windows with overlap, splitting on document structure (headings, sections, functions in code) and splitting on sentences or paragraphs. Pick by evaluating recall@k on a labelled set, not by intuition. Contextual Retrieval's cost example assumes 800-token chunks from 8k-token documents. That is one reasonable starting point, not a rule.

sections.heading: Metadata and access control
RAG vs long context vs fine-tuning
sections.body:
- **Long context.** Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval post notes that if your knowledge base is under about 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages), you can include the whole thing in the prompt, and prompt caching makes that cheaper and faster. Longer prompts have a cost of their own, though: 'Lost in the Middle' (Liu et al.) found U-shaped performance, worst when the relevant facts sit in the middle of a long context, and Anthropic describes context as a finite 'attention budget' that degrades as it grows (context rot).
- **RAG** wins when the corpus is larger than the context window or changes often, when you need citations to sources, or when different users may see different documents.
- **Fine-tuning** changes behaviour, style or format. It is a poor way to add or update facts: you can't cite the weights, and every update needs a new training run. The RAG paper's motivation was exactly that non-parametric memory can be updated and inspected.

keyPoints: RAG = parametric generator + non-parametric retrieved memory (Lewis et al., 2020).
Chunk size is a trade-off between precision and context; choose it by measuring recall@k.
Store source ID, version, tenant and permission metadata with every chunk.
Enforce access control as a retrieval filter or partition, never as a prompt instruction.
Under about 200K tokens, putting the whole knowledge base in the prompt (with caching) can beat RAG.
Fine-tune for behaviour and format, retrieve for facts that change or need citations.

gotchas.trap: Telling the model 'only use documents for tenant X' and retrieving across all tenants.
gotchas.correct: Filter or partition by tenant in the retrieval query so other tenants' chunks never reach the prompt (OWASP LLM08).

gotchas.trap: Fine-tuning a model on the product docs so it 'knows' them.
gotchas.correct: Use retrieval for facts that change or need citations. Fine-tuning shapes behaviour and needs a new run for every update.

gotchas.trap: Always building RAG, even for a 100-page handbook.
gotchas.correct: A small, stable corpus can go straight into the prompt with prompt caching. Measure before adding a retrieval layer.

lessons.lab: Take 20 documents from a real corpus and chunk them three ways (fixed 300 tokens with overlap, fixed 800 tokens, split by heading). For each chunk, store source_id, version and a tenant tag. Write 15 questions with known answer locations and compare recall@5 across the three chunkings.

lessons.title: Embeddings: Similarity, Dimensions and Versioning
lessons.summary: What embedding vectors capture, why normalisation makes cosine and dot product equivalent, how to shorten vectors safely, and why changing models means re-embedding everything.

sections.heading: What an embedding captures
sections.body: An embedding model maps text (or images, for multimodal models) to a fixed-length vector. Texts with similar meaning land close together, so 'reset my password' and 'I can't log in' can match without sharing a word. That is the strength of dense retrieval and also its weakness: exact identifiers such as error codes, SKUs and names carry little semantic signal, so dense retrieval can miss them. Lexical search (BM25) covers that gap.

sections.heading: Normalisation and distance
sections.body:
OpenAI's embeddings guide states that its embeddings 'are normalized to length 1'. For unit vectors:

- cosine similarity equals the dot product;
- cosine and Euclidean distance give the **same ranking**.

pgvector's README recommends inner product for best performance when vectors are normalized. In pgvector, `<->` is L2 distance, `<=>` is cosine distance and `<#>` returns the **negative** inner product, so `ORDER BY embedding <#> $1` ascending puts the most similar rows first. Multiply by −1 to recover the similarity.

sections.heading: Dimensions and shortening
sections.body:
OpenAI's `text-embedding-3-small` returns 1536 dimensions by default and `text-embedding-3-large` returns 3072. The API's `dimensions` parameter returns shorter vectors. This works because these models are trained so that the leading dimensions form a usable representation on their own, the idea behind Matryoshka Representation Learning (Kusupati et al.), which reported embeddings up to 14 times smaller at the same ImageNet accuracy.

Two rules:

- If you truncate vectors **yourself**, re-normalize them to length 1, or cosine and dot product stop agreeing.
- Index limits matter. At the time of writing, pgvector can store `vector` columns of up to 16,000 dimensions but can index only up to 2,000 with HNSW or IVFFlat (`halfvec` indexes up to 4,000). A 3072-dimension vector needs shortening or `halfvec` before you can index it. Check current limits before you design around them.

sections.heading: Choosing and versioning a model
sections.body:
Choose an embedding model by measuring recall@k on **your** labelled queries, considering cost per token, maximum input length, dimensions (storage and index size), languages and modalities. Provider lineups change often (Gemini, for example, has both text and multimodal embedding models), so pin the exact model ID.

**Vectors from different models, or from one model at different dimensions, are not comparable.** A model change means re-embedding the whole corpus and the queries with the new model. The usual safe migration: build a second index with the new model, compare both on the labelled set, switch reads over, then drop the old index. Store the model ID with each vector so mixed indexes are detectable.

keyPoints: Dense embeddings capture meaning; exact identifiers are better served by lexical search.
For unit-length vectors, cosine similarity = dot product, and cosine and Euclidean give the same ranking.
pgvector `<#>` is the negative inner product; ascending order gives the most similar rows first.
Shorten with the API's `dimensions` parameter; re-normalize if you truncate vectors yourself.
pgvector HNSW and IVFFlat index `vector` up to 2,000 dims (at the time of writing); `halfvec` up to 4,000.
Changing the embedding model or dimensions means re-embedding the whole corpus.

gotchas.trap: Embedding new documents with a new model and keeping old vectors from the previous model in the same index.
gotchas.correct: Vectors from different models live in different spaces. Re-embed everything, ideally into a parallel index, and switch over once it measures well.

gotchas.trap: Keeping only the first 512 values of each stored vector and still treating dot product as cosine.
gotchas.correct: Re-normalize truncated vectors to length 1, or request shorter vectors with the `dimensions` parameter.

gotchas.trap: Sorting pgvector `<#>` results in descending order to get the 'highest' similarity.
gotchas.correct: `<#>` returns the negative inner product. Sort ascending, and multiply by −1 to display the similarity.

lessons.lab: Embed 200 chunks at the full dimension size and with `dimensions` set to 256. Load both into pgvector, run the same 20 labelled queries against each and compare recall@10 and index size. Then truncate the full vectors to 256 values yourself without re-normalizing and watch cosine and dot-product rankings diverge.

lessons.title: Search: HNSW, BM25, Hybrid Fusion and Filters
lessons.summary: How approximate vector indexes work and are tuned, why lexical search still matters, how reciprocal rank fusion combines result lists, and how filters interact with approximate indexes.

sections.heading: HNSW in one page
sections.body:
Hierarchical Navigable Small World (Malkov and Yashunin) builds a hierarchy of proximity graphs. Each layer is a subset of the one below it, and each node's top layer is drawn with exponentially decaying probability. Search enters at the sparse top layer, greedily moves toward the query, and descends layer by layer. Complexity scales logarithmically.

pgvector's HNSW parameters (defaults at the time of writing):

- `m` = 16: connections per node. Higher means better recall, more memory and a slower build.
- `ef_construction` = 64: the candidate list size during build.
- `hnsw.ef_search` = 40: the candidate list size at query time. Raise it for better recall at the cost of latency.

HNSW is **approximate**: it trades a little recall for a large speed-up over exact search.

sections.heading: IVFFlat
BM25 and why lexical still matters
sections.body: BM25 is a lexical ranking function built on term frequency and inverse document frequency. It excels at exact strings: error codes, product numbers, names and rare jargon. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval post motivates BM25 with exactly this kind of query, a specific error code that embeddings miss. The BEIR benchmark found BM25 'a robust baseline' in zero-shot retrieval across diverse datasets, which is why any dense model you adopt should be compared against BM25 on your own data.

sections.heading: Hybrid search with reciprocal rank fusion
sections.body:
Hybrid search runs a dense and a lexical query and merges the two lists. Their raw scores are on incompatible scales (cosine similarity vs an unbounded BM25 score), so fuse by **rank**. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher, SIGIR 2009):

$$\mathrm{RRF}(d)=\sum_{r\in R}\frac{1}{k+r(d)}$$

The paper fixed k = 60 in a pilot study, found it near-optimal and found that the choice 'was not critical'. Worked example with k = 60: a document ranked 1st and 3rd scores 1/61 + 1/63 ≈ 0.032266. That just beats one ranked 2nd and 2nd, 2/62 ≈ 0.032258. A document in only one list at rank 1 scores 1/61 ≈ 0.016393. Appearing in both lists matters more than topping one.

pgvector's README suggests using it with Postgres full-text search and combining results with Reciprocal Rank Fusion or a cross-encoder.

sections.heading: Filters and approximate indexes

keyPoints: HNSW: layered proximity graphs searched top-down; tune `m`, `ef_construction` and query-time `ef_search`.
Raise `hnsw.ef_search` (or `ivfflat.probes`) to trade latency for recall.
Build IVFFlat after loading data; `probes` defaults to 1.
BM25 catches exact identifiers that embeddings miss and is a robust baseline (BEIR).
RRF fuses by rank: score = Σ 1/(k + rank), with k = 60 as the paper's default.
Approximate indexes filter after the scan; use iterative scans, B-tree or partial indexes, or partitioning.

gotchas.trap: Adding normalized cosine scores to raw BM25 scores to merge hybrid results.
gotchas.correct: The scales are incompatible. Fuse by rank with RRF, or rerank the union with a cross-encoder.

gotchas.trap: Expecting `WHERE tenant_id = $1 ... LIMIT 10` on an HNSW index to always return 10 rows.
gotchas.correct: The filter runs after the approximate scan, so rows can go missing. Enable iterative scans or use an index or partition that matches the filter.

gotchas.trap: Creating an IVFFlat index on an empty table and loading data afterwards.
gotchas.correct: IVFFlat learns its clusters from existing rows. Build it after the data is loaded.

lessons.lab: In Postgres with pgvector, index 50,000 chunks with HNSW and add a `tsvector` column for full-text search. Implement RRF (k = 60) over the top 50 of each. Then add `WHERE category = 'x'` for a category that is 5% of rows and observe short result sets; fix it with `SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order` and compare.

lessons.title: Reranking, Query Rewriting and Contextual Retrieval
lessons.summary: Second-stage reranking, rewriting queries so they match documents better, and Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval method with its measured results.

sections.heading: Two-stage retrieval and reranking
sections.body:
First-stage retrieval (vector, BM25 or hybrid) is fast and recall-oriented. A **reranker**, typically a cross-encoder that reads the query and each candidate together, then reorders a candidate set with far better precision, but it is too slow to run over the whole corpus. The BEIR benchmark found that reranking and late-interaction models achieve the best zero-shot performance on average, 'at high computational costs'.

The key design rule: **a reranker can only reorder what the first stage retrieved.** Contextual Retrieval retrieves the top 150 candidates, reranks them and passes the top 20 to the model. Retrieve wide, then narrow.

sections.heading: Query rewriting and HyDE
sections.body:
User queries are short, vague or conversational ('what about the second one?'). Rewriting options:

- **Standalone rewriting:** an LLM turns a follow-up into a self-contained query using the conversation history.
- **Decomposition:** split a multi-part question into sub-queries and retrieve for each.
- **HyDE** (Gao et al., 2022): an LLM writes a *hypothetical* answer document, you embed that document and use it to retrieve real ones. The fake document may contain errors, but it lives in the same 'answer-shaped' region of the vector space as the real documents.

Rewriting adds an LLM call to the latency of every query. Measure that it improves recall@k before shipping it.

sections.heading: Contextual Retrieval
sections.body:
Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval (September 2024) fixes chunks that have lost their context. For each chunk, an LLM receives the **whole document** plus the chunk and writes 50–100 tokens of chunk-specific context ('Please give a short succinct context to situate this chunk within the overall document...'). That context is **prepended to the chunk before embedding and before building the BM25 index**.

Results, measured as 1 − recall@20 (the top-20 retrieval failure rate):

| Configuration | Failure rate | Reduction |
|---|---|---|
| Baseline embeddings | 5.7% | — |
| Contextual Embeddings | 3.7% | −35% |
| + Contextual BM25 | 2.9% | −49% |
| + reranking | 1.9% | −67% |

Cost: because every chunk of a document shares the same long document prefix, **prompt caching** makes this cheap. The post estimates about $1.02 per million document tokens, one time, under its stated assumptions (800-token chunks, 8k-token documents). Treat the dollar figure as an illustration of that date's pricing.

keyPoints: Rerank a wide candidate set (for example, top 150) down to what the model sees (for example, top 20).
A reranker cannot recover documents the first stage never retrieved.
HyDE embeds an LLM-written hypothetical answer to retrieve real documents.
Contextual Retrieval prepends 50–100 tokens of LLM-generated, document-aware context to each chunk before embedding and BM25 indexing.
Contextual embeddings + contextual BM25 + reranking cut the top-20 failure rate by 67% in Anthropic's tests.
Prompt caching of the shared document makes per-chunk context generation affordable.

gotchas.trap: Reranking only the top 10 first-stage results and expecting big recall gains.
gotchas.correct: The reranker only reorders candidates. Retrieve a larger set (for example, 150) and rerank it down.

gotchas.trap: Applying Contextual Retrieval's generated context only to the embeddings.
gotchas.correct: The post prepends the context before embedding and before building the BM25 index; contextual BM25 adds further gains.

gotchas.trap: Generating chunk context with a fresh, uncached prompt containing the full document for every chunk.
gotchas.correct: Put the document first and cache it, so each chunk call only pays full price for the short chunk-specific part.

lessons.lab: Pick 10 long documents. Generate a 50–100 token context for each chunk with an LLM, using prompt caching on the document. Index plain and contextualized chunks side by side, then measure 1 − recall@20 on 30 labelled queries, with and without a reranker over the top 150.

lessons.title: Evaluating Retrieval: Metrics and Labelled Sets
lessons.summary: How to compute recall@k, precision@k, MRR and nDCG, which one fits which RAG design, and how to build a labelled query set you can trust.

sections.heading: Evaluate retrieval on its own
sections.body: A wrong RAG answer has two possible causes: the right chunk was never retrieved, or it was retrieved and the model misused it. End-to-end answer scores blur the two together. Measure **retrieval** separately, against a labelled set of queries with known relevant chunks or documents, before tuning prompts. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval work reports exactly such a retrieval-only metric, 1 − recall@20.

sections.heading: The metrics
sections.body:
For one query, with R = the set of relevant items and the top-k retrieved list:

- **recall@k** = (relevant items in the top k) / |R|. Did we find what exists?
- **precision@k** = (relevant items in the top k) / k. How much of what we pass is useful?
- **MRR** (mean reciprocal rank) = the mean over queries of 1/rank of the **first** relevant item (0 if none). Good when one right answer matters and it should be near the top.
- **nDCG@k** handles **graded** relevance and position: DCG = Σ gain(rel_i) / log2(i + 1), divided by the DCG of the ideal ordering. There are two common gain variants, rel and 2^rel − 1, so always state which one you use.

Worked example: graded relevances [3, 2, 0, 1] at positions 1–4, gain 2^rel − 1. DCG = 7/1 + 3/log2 3 + 0 + 1/log2 5 ≈ 9.3235. The ideal order [3, 2, 1, 0] gives IDCG ≈ 9.3928, so nDCG@4 ≈ 0.9926.

sections.heading: Match the metric to the design
sections.body:
- If the model receives the top 20 chunks, **recall@20** is the number that matters: order inside those 20 matters less than presence.
- If you show a single 'best answer' snippet, **MRR** or precision@1 fits.
- If position and graded usefulness both matter (search UIs, small context budgets), use **nDCG@k**.
- Track latency and cost next to quality, because reranking and rewriting add both.

sections.heading: Building a labelled set
sections.body:
1. **Sample real queries** from logs or support tickets, covering head and tail topics and the identifier-style queries that dense search misses.
2. **Label relevant documents or passages** with domain experts. Label at a level that survives re-chunking (document plus span) rather than only chunk IDs that change when you re-chunk.
3. **Augment with synthetic queries** (an LLM writes questions about a chunk) for coverage, but review them: synthetic queries tend to copy the chunk's wording and flatter lexical search.
4. **Hold out a test split.** Tune k, chunk size and fusion weights on a development split, and report on the untouched test split.
5. **Version the set** with the corpus snapshot, and re-run it on every change to the embedding model, chunker, index parameters or reranker.

Public benchmarks such as BEIR are useful for shortlisting models. Your own labelled set is what decides.

keyPoints: Measure retrieval separately from generation so failures can be attributed.
recall@k = found relevant / all relevant; precision@k = found relevant / k.
MRR averages 1/rank of the first relevant item (0 when none is found).
nDCG uses graded gains and a log2(i + 1) discount, normalised by the ideal ordering; state the gain variant.
Use recall@k for 'did the model get what it needed'; use MRR or nDCG when position matters.
Build the labelled set from real queries, label at a re-chunk-proof level, and keep a held-out split.

gotchas.trap: Judging retrieval changes only by end-to-end answer thumbs-up rates.
gotchas.correct: Score retrieval directly (recall@k and others) on a labelled set, then evaluate generation separately.

gotchas.trap: Tuning chunk size and k on the full labelled set and reporting that score as expected production quality.
gotchas.correct: Tune on a development split and report on a held-out test split, or the number is optimistic.

gotchas.trap: Comparing nDCG figures from two reports without checking the gain formula.
gotchas.correct: rel and 2^rel − 1 gains give different numbers. Fix and state one variant.

lessons.lab: Pull 50 real queries from logs, have a colleague label relevant document spans, and split them 30/20 into dev and test. Write a small script that computes recall@5, recall@20, precision@5, MRR and nDCG@10 (gain 2^rel − 1) for two retrieval configurations, tuning only on dev.

lessons.title: The tool-use loop
lessons.summary: How a model asks for a tool, how your code answers, and how to keep the loop correct when calls run in parallel, fail, or never stop.

sections.heading: Client tools and server tools
sections.body:
A tool call is a **request**, not an execution. The model emits a structured call and your code decides whether and how to run it. Anthropic splits tools into two kinds:

- **Client tools** run in your application: your own functions, plus Anthropic-schema tools such as `bash` and `text_editor`.
- **Server tools** run on Anthropic's side, for example web search, web fetch and code execution.

OpenAI and Gemini follow the same idea. Gemini's docs say it plainly: the model *doesn't* execute the function itself.

sections.heading: The round trip
sections.body:
1. Send the request with a `tools` array. Each tool has a `name`, a `description` and an `input_schema` (JSON Schema).
2. If the model wants a tool, the response ends with `stop_reason: "tool_use"` and contains one or more `tool_use` blocks, each with an `id`, `name` and `input`.
3. Append the assistant content to the conversation unchanged.
4. Send a **user** message containing a `tool_result` block per call, each with the matching `tool_use_id`.
5. Repeat until the model stops for another reason, such as `end_turn`.

OpenAI's Responses API uses the same shape with different names: `function_call` items carry a `call_id` and JSON-string `arguments`, and you reply with a `function_call_output` that carries the same `call_id`.

sections.heading: Placement rules that break loops
sections.body:
Anthropic's stop-reasons guide is strict about the follow-up message:

- It must contain **only** `tool_result` blocks, one for each `tool_use` in the previous turn.
- Keep the same `tools` array on the follow-up request.
- Adding anything after the `tool_result` blocks ends the assistant turn, so the model may stop instead of continuing the task.

If you want to add guidance, put it in the system prompt or in a later turn, not as stray text next to the results.

sections.heading: Parallel tool calls
sections.body: A single response can contain several `tool_use` blocks. Run them (concurrently if they are independent) and return **all** results together in one user message. If your tools have side effects that must happen in order, turn parallel calls off: Anthropic uses `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` on `tool_choice`, and OpenAI uses `parallel_tool_calls: false`.

sections.heading: Errors, turn limits and forcing
sections.body:
- **Errors.** When a call fails or the input is invalid, return a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` and an actionable message. The model reads it and can retry with corrected input. Do not crash the loop or silently drop the result.
- **Turn limits.** An agent loop needs stopping conditions, such as a maximum number of iterations, plus a budget for tokens or time. Without them a confused agent can loop and keep spending.
- **Forcing a tool.** `tool_choice` can be `auto`, `none`, `any` or a specific tool, but forced choice is **not supported on some current Claude models** and returns an error there. Check the model's docs. The portable approach is `auto` with a clear prompt and strict schemas, or structured outputs when you only need JSON.
- **Cost.** Tool definitions, `tool_use` blocks and `tool_result` blocks are all billed as input tokens, and enabling tools adds a system-prompt overhead.

keyPoints: The model requests tool calls; your code executes client tools and returns results.
Reply to `tool_use` with a user message holding only `tool_result` blocks, one per call, with matching ids.
Return every parallel result in a single message; disable parallel calls when order matters.
Report failures with `is_error: true` and a message the model can act on.
Always cap iterations and budget; forced `tool_choice` is not available on every model.

gotchas.trap: Adding a text note such as "here are the results" after the tool_result blocks.
gotchas.correct: Send only tool_result blocks; extra content after them ends the assistant turn.

gotchas.trap: Returning parallel results as several separate user messages.
gotchas.correct: Put every tool_result for that turn in one user message.

gotchas.trap: Assuming tool_choice any or a forced tool works on every model.
gotchas.correct: Some current Claude models reject forced tool choice; use auto plus strict schemas or structured outputs.

lessons.lab: Write a loop that calls a model with two tools (`get_weather` and `get_time`). Ask a question that needs both, log how many `tool_use` blocks arrive in one response, return both results in one message, then make one tool fail and confirm the model recovers from an `is_error` result. Add a max-iterations guard and test it with a tool that always errors.

lessons.title: Workflows versus agents
lessons.summary: The five composable workflow patterns, when an autonomous agent is worth its cost, and why the simplest design that works usually wins.

sections.heading: Two kinds of agentic system
sections.body:
Anthropic's *Building effective agents* draws one line:

- **Workflows** orchestrate models and tools through predefined code paths.
- **Agents** dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage.

Start with the simplest solution, often a single well-prompted call with retrieval. Add complexity only when it measurably improves results.

sections.heading: The five workflow patterns
sections.body:
| Pattern | Use when |
|---|---|
| Prompt chaining | The task is easily and cleanly decomposed into fixed subtasks. Add programmatic gates between steps. |
| Routing | Inputs fall into distinct categories that are better handled separately. |
| Parallelisation | Independent subtasks can run at once (**sectioning**), or several attempts can vote (**voting**). |
| Orchestrator-workers | You can't predict the subtasks needed; a central model breaks the task down at run time. |
| Evaluator-optimizer | There are clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement provides measurable value. |

The key difference between parallelisation and orchestrator-workers: in parallelisation the subtasks are fixed in code; an orchestrator decides them on the fly.

sections.heading: When to use an agent
sections.body: Agents fit open-ended problems where you cannot predict the number of steps or hard-code a path. The trade-offs are higher cost, higher latency and **compounding errors**, because each step builds on the last. Test agents extensively in sandboxed environments and give them stopping conditions and checkpoints for human review.

sections.heading: Principles
sections.body:
- **Simplicity.** Keep the design simple and frameworks optional; understand what the framework does underneath.
- **Transparency.** Show the agent's planning steps.
- **Agent-computer interface.** Put as much care into tool documentation and testing as into a human UI. Anthropic's example: the model made mistakes with relative paths, so the team changed the tool to always require absolute file paths, and the model then used it flawlessly.

keyPoints: Workflows follow predefined code paths; agents choose their own steps.
Chaining for fixed steps, routing for distinct categories, parallelisation for independent or voted work.
Orchestrator-workers when subtasks cannot be predicted; evaluator-optimizer when criteria are clear and iteration helps.
Agents trade cost and compounding errors for flexibility; sandbox and cap them.

gotchas.trap: Building a multi-agent framework for a task with three fixed steps.
gotchas.correct: Use a prompt chain; reach for agents only when the path cannot be predicted.

gotchas.trap: Calling any fan-out design orchestrator-workers.
gotchas.correct: If the subtasks are fixed in code it is parallelisation; orchestrator-workers decides subtasks at run time.

lessons.lab: Take one task (for example, answering a support email) and build it three ways: a single call, a routing workflow with two specialised prompts, and a small agent with two tools. Compare quality, cost and latency on 20 test emails and write down which you would ship.

lessons.title: Designing tools agents can use
lessons.summary: Names, descriptions, inputs and outputs that make tools easy for a model to choose and use, plus the safety properties that keep side effects under control.

sections.heading: Fewer, clearer tools
sections.body: Every tool competes for the model's attention. Anthropic's *Writing tools for agents* recommends a small set of targeted tools over thin wrappers around every API endpoint, and **namespacing** related tools (for example `asana_search`, `asana_projects_list`). The context-engineering post gives the test: if a human engineer can't say definitively which tool should be used in a situation, an agent can't be expected to do better. OpenAI's guide similarly suggests keeping the set of functions available at the start of a turn small.

sections.heading: Names, descriptions and inputs
sections.body:
- Names must match the provider's pattern; Anthropic allows letters, digits, underscores and hyphens.
- Write **detailed descriptions**: what the tool does, when to use it and when not to, what each parameter means, and caveats. Anthropic's docs ask for several sentences per tool.
- Use **unambiguous parameter names** such as `user_id` instead of `user`.
- Use strict JSON Schemas (types, enums, required fields) so bad inputs fail early.
- Design inputs to prevent mistakes (*poka-yoke*): requiring absolute paths removed a whole class of relative-path errors.

sections.heading: Outputs that respect the context window
sections.body: Return **high-signal** fields: names and readable identifiers rather than opaque UUIDs and raw internal metadata. Offer a `response_format` option such as concise or detailed. Paginate, filter and truncate large results with sensible defaults; Claude Code caps tool responses at a fixed token limit by default for this reason. When you truncate, say so and tell the model how to get more.

sections.heading: Actionable errors
sections.body: An error message is a prompt. "Error 400" teaches the model nothing; "`start_date` must be ISO 8601, for example 2026-03-14" lets it fix the call on the next turn.

sections.heading: Idempotency and least privilege
sections.body:
Agents retry, and approvals do not guarantee exactly-once execution. Make side-effecting tools **idempotent**, for example by accepting an idempotency key so a repeated `issue_refund` does not refund twice.

Apply **least privilege**: OWASP's LLM06 *Excessive Agency* covers excessive functionality, permissions and autonomy. Give each tool the narrowest scope and credentials it needs, prefer read-only tools where possible, and require human approval for high-impact actions. A system-prompt instruction such as "never delete" is not an access control. MCP's spec says the same from the protocol side: tools represent arbitrary code execution and need user consent.

keyPoints: Prefer a few well-scoped, namespaced tools over many overlapping ones.
Descriptions and parameter names are prompts; make them detailed and unambiguous.
Return concise, high-signal output with pagination and truncation.
Write errors the model can act on.
Make side effects idempotent and give tools only the permissions they need.

gotchas.trap: Returning the full raw API payload so the model has everything.
gotchas.correct: Return the fields the task needs, paginate, and offer a detailed mode on request.

gotchas.trap: Relying on the system prompt to stop destructive actions.
gotchas.correct: Enforce limits in the tool and its credentials, and gate high-impact actions behind approval.

lessons.lab: Pick an internal API with at least five endpoints. Design two to three agent-facing tools for it: write the names, descriptions and schemas, add a `response_format` parameter and pagination, and make the one write action idempotent. Then ask a colleague to pick the right tool for ten tasks using only your descriptions.

lessons.title: Model Context Protocol
lessons.summary: MCP's participants and primitives, its two transports, how authorization works, and what changed in the stateless 2026-07-28 revision.

sections.heading: Hosts, clients and servers
sections.body:
MCP is JSON-RPC 2.0 between three participants:

- **Host**: the LLM application the user runs, such as an IDE or chat app.
- **Client**: a connector inside the host. There is **one client per server**.
- **Server**: a service that exposes context and capabilities.

An IDE connected to three MCP servers is one host with three clients.

sections.heading: Primitives
sections.body:
Servers offer three features:

- **Resources**: context and data for the user or model to use.
- **Prompts**: templated messages and workflows for users.
- **Tools**: functions for the AI model to execute.

On the client side, the 2026-07-28 spec lists **Elicitation** (asking the user for input) as the active feature. Sampling, Roots and Logging still work but are **deprecated**: migrate to direct LLM API calls, tool parameters or configuration, and stderr or OpenTelemetry respectively.

sections.heading: Transports
sections.body:
- **stdio**: the client launches the server as a subprocess and they exchange newline-delimited JSON-RPC on stdin and stdout. Anything else written to stdout corrupts the stream, so log to stderr.
- **Streamable HTTP**: each message is an HTTP POST to a single MCP endpoint, and replies arrive as a JSON object or a request-scoped SSE stream.

The older HTTP+SSE transport is deprecated.

sections.heading: Authorization
sections.body:
Authorization is optional. HTTP transports should follow the spec; stdio servers should not and instead get credentials from the environment. For HTTP:

- The MCP server is an **OAuth 2.1 resource server** and must publish Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728) so clients can discover the authorization server.
- Clients use PKCE and send the `resource` parameter (RFC 8707) so the token is bound to that server.
- Tokens go in the `Authorization: Bearer` header and must not be put in the URI query string.
- Servers must validate that the token was issued for them (audience) and must not accept or pass through other tokens.
- Insufficient scope returns 403 `insufficient_scope`, followed by a step-up flow.

Dynamic Client Registration is deprecated in favour of Client ID Metadata Documents.

sections.heading: What changed in 2026-07-28
sections.body:
The 2026-07-28 revision made MCP **stateless**:

- The `initialize` handshake is removed. Every request carries the protocol version and client capabilities in `_meta`.
- Servers must implement `server/discover`.
- Protocol sessions and the `Mcp-Session-Id` header are removed. State that spans calls uses explicit handles that the server mints and the model passes back as tool arguments.
- Multi round-trip requests replace server-initiated requests: a server returns `resultType: "input_required"` and the client retries with the answers.
- Servers should list tools in a deterministic order, which helps prompt-cache hits.

MCP revisions change often; check the spec's changelog before relying on protocol details.

sections.heading: Security principles
sections.body: The spec puts the burden on the host: obtain explicit user consent before exposing user data to servers and before invoking any tool. Tools represent arbitrary code execution, and tool annotations (such as a read-only hint) should be treated as untrusted unless they come from a trusted server.

keyPoints: One host, one client per server, many servers.
Resources are data, prompts are user templates, tools are model-invoked functions.
stdio for local subprocesses, Streamable HTTP for remote servers.
Remote auth is OAuth 2.1 with audience-bound tokens and no token passthrough.
Since 2026-07-28 MCP is stateless: no initialize, no session header.

gotchas.trap: Teaching Sampling and Roots as current client features.
gotchas.correct: In 2026-07-28 they are deprecated; Elicitation is the active client feature.

gotchas.trap: Printing debug logs to stdout in a stdio server.
gotchas.correct: stdout carries the protocol; log to stderr.

gotchas.trap: Forwarding the user's upstream token through the MCP server.
gotchas.correct: Servers must only accept tokens issued for them and must not pass tokens through.

lessons.lab: Build a tiny stdio MCP server with one tool and one resource using an official SDK, connect it to an MCP-capable host, and confirm the tool appears. Then add a `print()` to stdout and observe the failure, and move the log to stderr.

lessons.title: Context engineering for agents
lessons.summary: Keeping a long-running agent's context small and relevant with just-in-time retrieval, compaction, note-taking, sub-agents and well-designed memory.

sections.heading: Context is a budget
sections.body: As an agent works, its context fills with tool calls and results, and quality can degrade as the window fills. Anthropic's *Effective context engineering* frames the goal as finding the smallest set of high-signal tokens that gets the job done. Write system prompts at the **right altitude**: specific enough to guide behaviour, not a brittle list of hard-coded rules.

sections.heading: Just-in-time retrieval
sections.body: Instead of loading everything up front, give the agent **lightweight references** (file paths, URLs, query handles) and tools to load the details when needed. This keeps the window small and lets the agent explore progressively.

sections.heading: Compaction and tool-result clearing
sections.body: **Compaction** summarises a long conversation and continues in a fresh window with the summary. **Tool-result clearing**, removing old raw tool outputs the agent no longer needs, is described as one of the safest forms. Providers now offer managed compaction (for example Anthropic's on-demand compaction beta and OpenAI's `context_management` options); check current docs for names and defaults. Compaction is a context-window tool, **not** long-term memory.

sections.heading: Notes and memory
sections.body:
**Structured note-taking**, such as an agent maintaining a NOTES.md or progress file, lets it persist state outside the window and pick up after a reset. Anthropic's *Components of agent memory* (2026) describes layers from raw transcripts to memory notes, consolidated representations such as wikis, and finally the context injected into a prompt. Its findings include:

- Organising memory as one page per entity preserved facts that a single shared table lost.
- A rule to record only failures reduced the benefit of memory.
- A note can be **wrong from the start or drift** as things change, and later sessions still trust it. An offline consolidation pass ("dreaming") that checks notes against the original transcripts catches these errors.

sections.heading: Sub-agents and long-running tasks
sections.body: A lead agent can hand focused sub-tasks to **sub-agents**, each with its own clean context window, and receive condensed summaries back (Anthropic cites often 1,000 to 2,000 tokens). This keeps the lead's context clean and allows parallel exploration, at the cost of more total tokens. For tasks that span many sessions, combine progress notes, checkpoints and clear stopping criteria.

keyPoints: Treat context as a finite budget of high-signal tokens.
Load details just in time through references and tools.
Clear stale tool results and compact long histories; compaction is not memory.
Persist state in notes or memory, and verify notes against source transcripts.
Sub-agents explore in clean windows and return short summaries.

gotchas.trap: Treating a compacted summary as the agent's long-term memory.
gotchas.correct: Compaction manages one context window; persist durable facts in a memory or notes store.

gotchas.trap: Assuming more context is always better.
gotchas.correct: Irrelevant tokens dilute attention; keep only what the next step needs.

lessons.lab: Run an agent on a 30-step task and log context size per turn. Add tool-result clearing for outputs older than five turns and a NOTES.md the agent updates each step, then compare token use and task success with and without the changes.

lessons.title: Why evals: regression safety and a first eval set
lessons.summary: Evals turn "it seems better" into a repeatable measurement. This lesson covers the vocabulary of an eval, why every prompt or model change needs a regression suite, and how to build the first 20 to 50 tasks from real traffic and real failures.

sections.heading: The vocabulary of an eval
sections.body:
Anthropic's guide to agent evals uses a small set of terms that apply to any LLM feature:

- **Task**: one input plus its success criteria.
- **Trial**: one attempt at a task. Model output varies, so you usually run several trials per task.
- **Grader**: the logic that scores a trial (code, a model, or a human).
- **Transcript** (also trace or trajectory): the full record of a trial, including tool calls and intermediate steps.
- **Outcome**: the final state of the environment, such as whether the refund really exists in the database. It is not what the agent *says* it did.
- **Evaluation harness**: the code that runs tasks, collects transcripts and applies graders.
- **Agent harness**: the scaffolding around the model (prompts, tools, loop). When you evaluate an agent you are measuring harness plus model together.

sections.heading: Why evals are regression safety
sections.body:
LLM features fail quietly. A one-line prompt edit, a new model snapshot or a tool description change can fix the case you were looking at and break five you were not. Without an eval, the only signal is user complaints days later.

OpenAI's prompting guide puts it as a rule of practice: treat prompts as application code: version them, review prompt changes in the same pull requests as the behaviour they support, and run evaluation checks as part of every deployment. The same applies to model upgrades. Pin a model snapshot (every Claude model ID is a pinned snapshot) and only move to a new one after the regression suite passes on it.

sections.heading: Capability evals vs regression evals
sections.body:
The two suites answer different questions:

| | Capability eval | Regression eval |
|---|---|---|
| Question | Can the system do this yet? | Did we break anything? |
| Expected pass rate | Starts low | Should sit near 100% |
| What a drop means | Normal: the work is hard | A real regression to investigate |

When a capability suite saturates (it passes reliably for several releases), it **graduates** into the regression suite and you write new, harder capability tasks.

sections.heading: Building the set from real traffic
sections.body:
You do not need thousands of tasks to start. Anthropic's guidance is to begin with **20 to 50 tasks drawn from real failures**: bug reports, support escalations, thumbs-down responses and production traces.

A good task is **unambiguous**: two domain experts reading it would agree on pass or fail. If they would argue, fix the task or the criteria before adding it.

Cover both directions:

- **Should-happen** cases: the assistant answers, calls the right tool, extracts the right field.
- **Should-not-happen** cases: the assistant declines an out-of-scope request, does not call the refund tool for an ineligible order, does not invent a citation.

A suite of only happy-path cases rewards a system that does everything, including the things it should not do.

sections.heading: Grade outcomes, not the path
sections.body:
For agents there are usually several valid ways to reach a goal. A grader that checks for one exact sequence of tool calls fails correct solutions and teaches you to overfit the prompt. Grade the **outcome**: the booking exists with the right dates, the file compiles and the tests pass, the ticket has the correct status.

Equally, do not grade the agent's own claim ("I have booked the flight"). Check the environment.

sections.heading: Read the transcripts
sections.body: Aggregate scores hide grading bugs. Read a sample of transcripts every time a number moves, and especially when a task scores **0% over many trials**. That pattern usually means the task or grader is broken (an impossible requirement, a wrong expected answer, a grader that cannot parse valid output), not that the model is hopeless. Anthropic reports a CORE-Bench result moving from 42% to about 95% for the same model once grading bugs were fixed.

keyPoints: A task is input plus success criteria; a trial is one attempt; a grader scores it; the outcome is the real end state.
Run a regression suite on every prompt, tool or model change, and pin model snapshots so changes are deliberate.
Capability evals start low; regression evals sit near 100%; saturated capability tasks graduate into regression.
Start with 20 to 50 unambiguous tasks from real failures, including should-not-happen cases.
Grade the outcome, not the exact path or the agent's claim, and read transcripts when numbers move.

gotchas.trap: Wait until you have a large synthetic benchmark before evaluating anything.
gotchas.correct: Start small with 20 to 50 tasks taken from real failures and traffic, then grow the set.

gotchas.trap: Check that the agent called tools in the expected order.
gotchas.correct: Check the final environment state; different valid paths should pass.

gotchas.trap: A task that scores 0% across many trials proves the model cannot do it.
gotchas.correct: Read the transcripts first; a 0% task is usually a broken task or grader.

lessons.lab: Pull 30 recent thumbs-down or escalated conversations from your logs. For each, write the input and a pass/fail criterion that a colleague would grade the same way. Add at least 5 should-not-happen cases. Run the current prompt over the set three times and read every failing transcript before you trust the score.
