flashcards.front: Which three fields does every Anthropic Messages request require?
flashcards.back: `model`, `max_tokens` and `messages`. The system prompt is a separate top-level `system` field.

flashcards.front: Who holds conversation history with the Anthropic Messages API?
flashcards.back: Your application. The API is stateless, so you resend the full history on every call.

flashcards.front: Where does a Claude refusal show up?
flashcards.back: As an HTTP 200 with `stop_reason: "refusal"`; `stop_details` is populated only for refusals.

flashcards.front: What should you do on `stop_reason: "pause_turn"`?
flashcards.back: A server-tool loop hit its iteration limit. Send the response content back unchanged so it can continue.

flashcards.front: Which two Claude stop reasons mean truncated output?
flashcards.back: `max_tokens` and `model_context_window_exceeded`.

flashcards.front: Common cause of an empty 2-3 token `end_turn` on Claude?
flashcards.back: A text block placed right after `tool_result` blocks. Fix the message shape; do not retry unchanged.

flashcards.front: In a Claude stream, where does `stop_reason` arrive?
flashcards.back: In the `message_delta` event. It is null in `message_start`.

flashcards.front: Can a streamed Claude response fail after HTTP 200?
flashcards.back: Yes. An error event such as `overloaded_error` can arrive mid-stream.

flashcards.front: How should you read text from an OpenAI Responses result?
flashcards.back: `response.output_text`, or iterate `output` by item type. Never assume `output[0]` is the message.

flashcards.front: How do you stop OpenAI from storing Responses?
flashcards.back: Set `store: false`. Responses are stored for 30 days by default.

flashcards.front: What must you re-send each turn with Gemini `previous_interaction_id`?
flashcards.back: `tools`, `system_instruction` and `generation_config`: they are interaction-scoped.

flashcards.front: How many few-shot examples does Anthropic suggest, and how wrapped?
flashcards.back: 3 to 5 diverse examples, each in `<example>` tags.

flashcards.front: Long documents and the question: which order?
flashcards.back: Documents first, question last. Anthropic reports up to 30 percent better responses on complex inputs.

flashcards.front: Does prefilling the assistant turn still work on current Claude and Gemini 3+?
flashcards.back: No. It returns a 400. Use structured outputs for format.

flashcards.front: Lever for consistency now that temperature is rejected or ignored?
flashcards.back: Constrain output (schema, enums), give clear examples, and measure with repeated-trial evals.

flashcards.front: How do you control reasoning depth on current Claude models?
flashcards.back: `output_config.effort` with adaptive thinking. Manual `budget_tokens` thinking is not accepted on later models.

flashcards.front: JSON mode vs structured outputs?
flashcards.back: JSON mode guarantees valid JSON only. Structured outputs constrain the output to your JSON Schema.

flashcards.front: OpenAI strict mode: how is an optional field written?
flashcards.back: Keep it in `required` and give it a union type with `null`. Also set `additionalProperties: false` on every object.

flashcards.front: Name schema keywords Anthropic structured outputs do not support.
flashcards.back: Numeric bounds (`minimum`/`maximum`/`multipleOf`), string lengths (`minLength`/`maxLength`), recursive schemas and external `$ref`.

flashcards.front: What does Gemini do with `minLength` or `maxLength` in a schema?
flashcards.back: Silently strips them. Enforce lengths in application code.

flashcards.front: What happens to the Claude prompt cache when `output_config.format` changes?
flashcards.back: It is invalidated. Keep schemas stable across requests.

flashcards.front: Repair strategy for a Pydantic `ValidationError` on complete output?
flashcards.back: Retry once with the validation error in the prompt, then fail loudly or queue for review.

flashcards.front: What is context rot?
flashcards.back: Recall degrades as context grows, because attention is a finite budget over n² token pairs.

flashcards.front: "Lost in the Middle" finding?
flashcards.back: Performance is U-shaped: best when key information is at the start or end, worst in the middle.

flashcards.front: When can you skip RAG per Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval post?
flashcards.back: When the knowledge base is under about 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages): put it in the prompt.

flashcards.front: Cheaper lever to try before moving to a bigger Claude model?
flashcards.back: Raise the effort level. Anthropic notes tuning effort is often better than switching models.

flashcards.front: How should a client treat a Claude 429 with `enforced_spend_limit_reached`?
flashcards.back: Do not retry: it has no `retry-after` and keeps failing. Alert and fail over.

flashcards.front: What two kinds of memory does RAG combine (Lewis et al., 2020)?
flashcards.back: Parametric memory (the generator's weights) and non-parametric memory (an external index searched by a retriever).

flashcards.front: RAG-Sequence vs RAG-Token?
flashcards.back: RAG-Sequence uses the same retrieved passages for the whole output; RAG-Token can use different passages for each generated token.

flashcards.front: Main trade-off in chunk size?
flashcards.back: Small chunks are precise but lose context; large chunks keep context but dilute the embedding and use more prompt budget. Choose by measuring recall@k.

flashcards.front: Which metadata should every chunk carry?
flashcards.back: Source document ID, version and location (for citations and re-indexing), tenant and permission tags (for access control), and filterable attributes.

flashcards.front: Where should multi-tenant access control be enforced in RAG?
flashcards.back: In the retrieval layer: permission-aware filtering or strict partitioning, so other tenants' chunks never reach the prompt (OWASP LLM08).

flashcards.front: When does Anthropic suggest skipping RAG altogether?
flashcards.back: When the knowledge base is under about 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages): include it all in the prompt, using prompt caching.

flashcards.front: RAG or fine-tuning for facts that change weekly and need citations?
flashcards.back: RAG. Its index can be updated and cited; fine-tuning changes behaviour and needs retraining for every update.

flashcards.front: What did 'Lost in the Middle' find?
flashcards.back: Performance is U-shaped across context position: best when relevant information is at the start or end, worst in the middle.

flashcards.front: For unit-length embeddings, how do cosine similarity and dot product relate?
flashcards.back: They are equal, and cosine and Euclidean distance give the same ranking. OpenAI's embeddings are normalized to length 1.

flashcards.front: You truncated embedding vectors yourself. What must you do next?
flashcards.back: Re-normalize them to length 1 (or request shorter vectors with the API's `dimensions` parameter instead).

flashcards.front: What makes embedding truncation work (Matryoshka Representation Learning)?
flashcards.back: Training so that the leading dimensions form a usable representation on their own; the paper reports up to 14 times smaller embeddings at the same ImageNet accuracy.

flashcards.front: Can you mix vectors from two embedding models in one index?
flashcards.back: No. They live in different vector spaces; re-embed the whole corpus (and the queries) with the new model.

flashcards.front: What does pgvector's `<#>` operator return?
flashcards.back: The negative inner product. Order ascending for the most similar rows first, and multiply by −1 for the similarity.

flashcards.front: pgvector operators for L2 and cosine distance?
flashcards.back: `<->` is L2 (Euclidean) distance; `<=>` is cosine distance.

flashcards.front: pgvector's maximum indexable dimensions for `vector` with HNSW or IVFFlat (at the time of writing)?
flashcards.back: 2,000 dimensions (`halfvec` up to 4,000). Larger vectors can be stored but not indexed with those methods.

flashcards.front: How does an HNSW search proceed?
flashcards.back: It starts at the sparse top layer of a hierarchy of proximity graphs, moves greedily toward the query, and descends layer by layer, with logarithmic complexity scaling.

flashcards.front: Which pgvector setting raises HNSW recall at query time?
flashcards.back: `hnsw.ef_search` (default 40): a larger candidate list gives better recall at higher latency.

flashcards.front: When should you build an IVFFlat index?
flashcards.back: After loading data, because its clusters (`lists`) are learned from existing rows; tune `ivfflat.probes`, which defaults to 1.

flashcards.front: Why can a filtered HNSW query return fewer rows than its LIMIT?
flashcards.back: Approximate indexes apply the filter after the index scan. Fix with iterative index scans, a B-tree or partial index, or partitioning.

flashcards.front: Reciprocal Rank Fusion formula?
flashcards.back: RRF(d) = Σ over result lists of 1 / (k + rank of d), with k = 60 in Cormack et al. (2009).

flashcards.front: Why fuse hybrid results by rank rather than by score?
flashcards.back: Dense similarity and BM25 scores are on incompatible scales; RRF uses only ranks, so no score calibration is needed.

flashcards.front: What is BM25 good at that dense embeddings are not?
flashcards.back: Exact lexical matches such as error codes, product IDs, names and rare terms. BEIR found it a robust zero-shot baseline.

flashcards.front: What is HyDE?
flashcards.back: Query rewriting where an LLM writes a hypothetical answer document, which is embedded and used to retrieve real documents.

flashcards.front: What does Contextual Retrieval prepend to each chunk?
flashcards.back: 50–100 tokens of LLM-generated, chunk-specific context written from the whole document, added before embedding and before BM25 indexing.

flashcards.front: Contextual Retrieval results (1 − recall@20)?
flashcards.back: Baseline 5.7%; contextual embeddings 3.7% (−35%); plus contextual BM25 2.9% (−49%); plus reranking 1.9% (−67%).

flashcards.front: Why can a reranker not fix poor first-stage recall?
flashcards.back: It only reorders the candidates it is given. Retrieve wide (for example, top 150) and rerank down (for example, to 20).

flashcards.front: recall@k vs precision@k?
flashcards.back: recall@k = relevant items in the top k / all relevant items; precision@k = relevant items in the top k / k.

flashcards.front: How is MRR computed?
flashcards.back: The mean over queries of 1 / rank of the first relevant result, counting 0 when no relevant result is retrieved.

flashcards.front: What does nDCG add over recall and precision?
flashcards.back: Graded relevance and position discounting (gain / log2(i + 1)), normalised by the ideal ordering. State whether the gain is rel or 2^rel − 1.

flashcards.front: Three rules for a retrieval labelled set?
flashcards.back: Use real queries labelled by experts, label at a level that survives re-chunking, and keep a held-out test split separate from tuning.

flashcards.front: What does `stop_reason: "tool_use"` tell your code?
flashcards.back: The model wants one or more tools run. Execute the requested client tools and reply with matching `tool_result` blocks.

flashcards.front: What must the user message after a `tool_use` turn contain on the Claude API?
flashcards.back: Only `tool_result` blocks, one per `tool_use`, each with the matching `tool_use_id`. Extra content after them ends the assistant turn.

flashcards.front: How do you return the results of three parallel tool calls?
flashcards.back: All three `tool_result` blocks in a single user message, each matched to its call id.

flashcards.front: How do you turn off parallel tool calls on Claude and on OpenAI?
flashcards.back: Claude: `disable_parallel_tool_use: true` inside `tool_choice`. OpenAI: `parallel_tool_calls: false`.

flashcards.front: How should a tool report a failure to the model?
flashcards.back: Return a `tool_result` with `is_error: true` and an actionable message, so the model can correct the input and retry.

flashcards.front: Client tools vs server tools (Anthropic)?
flashcards.back: Client tools run in your application. Server tools such as web search and code execution run on Anthropic's side.

flashcards.front: Which parts of tool use are billed as input tokens?
flashcards.back: Tool definitions, `tool_use` blocks and `tool_result` blocks, plus a tool-use system-prompt overhead.

flashcards.front: In OpenAI function calling, how is a result linked to its call?
flashcards.back: The `function_call_output` item carries the same `call_id` as the `function_call` item.

flashcards.front: What is the portable alternative when forced `tool_choice` is unsupported on a model?
flashcards.back: Use `auto` with a clear prompt and strict schemas, or structured outputs if you only need JSON.

flashcards.front: Workflow vs agent (Building effective agents)?
flashcards.back: Workflows follow predefined code paths. Agents dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage.

flashcards.front: When does prompt chaining fit?
flashcards.back: When the task can be easily and cleanly decomposed into fixed subtasks, optionally with programmatic gates between steps.

flashcards.front: When does routing fit?
flashcards.back: When inputs fall into distinct categories that are better handled separately, for example by different prompts or models.

flashcards.front: Two variants of the parallelisation pattern?
flashcards.back: Sectioning (independent subtasks run at once) and voting (the same task run several times for diverse outputs or consensus).

flashcards.front: Orchestrator-workers vs parallelisation?
flashcards.back: Orchestrator-workers decides the subtasks at run time; parallelisation runs subtasks fixed in code.

flashcards.front: When does evaluator-optimizer fit?
flashcards.back: When there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement provides measurable value.

flashcards.front: Main costs of autonomous agents?
flashcards.back: Higher cost and latency, and compounding errors; test them in sandboxes with stopping conditions.

flashcards.front: What is the poka-yoke example in Building effective agents?
flashcards.back: The model erred with relative paths, so the tool was changed to always require absolute file paths.

flashcards.front: Why namespace tools (for example `asana_search`)?
flashcards.back: It groups related tools and helps the model tell similar tools from different services apart.

flashcards.front: How should a tool handle a very large result?
flashcards.back: Return high-signal fields, paginate or truncate with sensible defaults, say when output is truncated, and optionally offer concise vs detailed formats.

flashcards.front: Why give side-effecting tools an idempotency key?
flashcards.back: Agents retry and approvals do not guarantee exactly-once execution; the key stops duplicate effects such as double refunds.

flashcards.front: Which OWASP 2025 entry covers tools with too many permissions?
flashcards.back: LLM06 Excessive Agency: excessive functionality, permissions or autonomy.

flashcards.front: MCP participants?
flashcards.back: Host (the LLM app), client (one connector per server, inside the host) and server.

flashcards.front: MCP server primitives?
flashcards.back: Resources (context and data), prompts (templated messages and workflows for users) and tools (functions the model executes).

flashcards.front: Active MCP client feature in 2026-07-28, and what is deprecated?
flashcards.back: Elicitation is active. Sampling, Roots and Logging are deprecated but still work.

flashcards.front: The two MCP transports?
flashcards.back: stdio (client-launched subprocess, newline-delimited JSON-RPC) and Streamable HTTP (POSTs to one endpoint, JSON or request-scoped SSE replies).

flashcards.front: Where must logs go in a stdio MCP server?
flashcards.back: stderr. stdout carries the protocol messages.

flashcards.front: What role does a remote MCP server play in OAuth?
flashcards.back: An OAuth 2.1 resource server. It publishes Protected Resource Metadata and validates that tokens were issued for it.

flashcards.front: What is token passthrough and is it allowed in MCP?
flashcards.back: Forwarding a token that was not issued for the server. It is forbidden: servers must not accept or transit other tokens.

flashcards.front: What replaced `initialize` and sessions in MCP 2026-07-28?
flashcards.back: Each request carries protocol version and client capabilities in `_meta`; servers implement `server/discover`; cross-call state uses server-minted handles.

flashcards.front: What is tool-result clearing?
flashcards.back: Removing old raw tool outputs from the context; Anthropic calls it one of the safest forms of compaction.

flashcards.front: Is compaction long-term memory?
flashcards.back: No. It manages one context window. Durable facts belong in notes or a memory store.

flashcards.front: Why use sub-agents?
flashcards.back: Each explores in a clean context window and returns a condensed summary (often 1,000 to 2,000 tokens), keeping the lead agent's context clean.

flashcards.front: What is just-in-time retrieval?
flashcards.back: Keeping lightweight references (paths, URLs, handles) in context and loading the details through tools only when needed.

flashcards.front: What is the risk of wrong or drifting memory notes?
flashcards.back: A note that is wrong from the start, or drifts as things change, is trusted in later sessions. Mitigate by verifying notes against the source transcripts, for example in a consolidation pass.

flashcards.front: In eval vocabulary, what are a task, a trial and a grader?
flashcards.back: A task is an input plus its success criteria. A trial is one attempt at the task. A grader is the logic (code, model or human) that scores a trial.

flashcards.front: What is the difference between an eval's transcript and its outcome?
flashcards.back: The transcript (trace, trajectory) is the record of what happened during a trial. The outcome is the final environment state, such as whether the booking really exists, not what the agent claimed.

flashcards.front: What does pass@k measure?
flashcards.back: The probability that at least one of k trials succeeds: 1 − (1 − p)^k. With p = 0.75, pass@3 ≈ 0.984.

flashcards.front: What does pass^k measure, and when should you report it?
flashcards.back: The probability that all k trials succeed: p^k. Use it when every attempt must succeed, such as a customer-facing agent. With p = 0.75, pass^3 ≈ 0.42.

flashcards.front: Capability eval vs regression eval: expected pass rates?
flashcards.back: Capability evals start at a low pass rate (can we do this yet?). Regression evals should sit near 100% (did we break anything?).

flashcards.front: What happens to a capability eval that has saturated?
flashcards.back: It graduates into the regression suite, and you write new, harder capability tasks.

flashcards.front: How should you start an eval set, per Anthropic's agent-evals guidance?
flashcards.back: With 20 to 50 tasks drawn from real failures and traffic, covering both should-happen and should-not-happen cases.

flashcards.front: What makes a good eval task?
flashcards.back: It is unambiguous: two domain experts would agree on whether a given result passes or fails.

flashcards.front: Code-based graders: strengths and weakness?
flashcards.back: Fast, cheap and reproducible, but brittle: they can reject valid answers phrased differently. Best for checkable properties such as schema, labels and test results.

flashcards.front: Model-based graders (LLM-as-judge): strengths and weaknesses?
flashcards.back: Flexible for open-ended output and scalable, but non-deterministic, biased, and must be calibrated against human labels.

flashcards.front: What role do human graders play in an eval program?
flashcards.back: They are the gold standard but slow, so they label calibration sets, resolve ambiguous cases and audit samples rather than grading everything.

flashcards.front: What is position bias in a pairwise LLM judge, and the standard fix?
flashcards.back: The judge favours an answer because of where it appears. Fix: run both orders and aggregate (Balanced Position Calibration), counting inconsistent verdicts as ties.

flashcards.front: What is verbosity bias?
flashcards.back: A judge's tendency to prefer longer answers even when they are not better. Counter it in the rubric and check whether win rate tracks length.

flashcards.front: What did Panickssery, Bowman and Feng find about self-preference?
flashcards.back: LLM evaluators favour their own generations, and a model's ability to recognise its own outputs correlates linearly with how strongly it favours them.

flashcards.front: How well did a strong LLM judge agree with humans in the MT-Bench study?
flashcards.back: Over 80% agreement with human preferences, about the same level as agreement between humans.

flashcards.front: Name the three calibration strategies from "Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators".
flashcards.back: Balanced Position Calibration (swap order and aggregate), Multiple Evidence Calibration (reasoning before verdict, several samples) and Human-in-the-Loop Calibration.

flashcards.front: How do you validate an LLM judge before using it as a gate?
flashcards.back: Have experts label a sample with the same rubric, compare judge-human agreement with human-human agreement, fix the rubric from disagreements, and re-calibrate when the judge or rubric changes.

flashcards.front: Standard error of a pass/fail eval score?
flashcards.back: SE = sqrt(p(1 − p) / n). The 95% CI is mean ± 1.96 × SE. Example: 0.82 on 400 questions gives SE ≈ 0.019 and CI ≈ [0.782, 0.858].

flashcards.front: When do you need a clustered standard error?
flashcards.back: When questions share a unit (several questions per passage, translations of one item). The clustered SE can be about 3× the naive one; report the number of clusters.

flashcards.front: Why use paired differences to compare two prompts on the same questions?
flashcards.back: Per-question scores are positively correlated, so SE(A − B) = sqrt(SE_A² + SE_B² − 2·SE_A·SE_B·Corr) is smaller than treating them as independent. Overlapping CIs are not a valid test.

flashcards.front: Why not lower the temperature to make eval runs less noisy?
flashcards.back: It changes the system you are measuring, and many current models reject or ignore sampling parameters. Run repeated trials and average instead.

flashcards.front: Roughly how many questions per arm to detect a 3-point difference near 80% accuracy (α 0.05, power 0.8, independent)?
flashcards.back: About 2,800 per arm (using p(1 − p) = 0.16). Pairing on the same questions reduces the number; a 200-item suite cannot resolve it.

flashcards.front: A task scores 0% across many trials. What does that usually mean?
flashcards.back: The task or grader is broken. Read the transcripts before concluding the model cannot do it.

flashcards.front: What is a guardrail metric in an A/B test of an LLM feature?
flashcards.back: A metric the change is not meant to improve but must not worsen, such as p95 latency, cost per request, refusal rate or safety flags, with a pre-set rollback threshold.

flashcards.front: Why compare a canary against a concurrent control instead of last week's numbers?
flashcards.back: Before/after comparisons are confounded by traffic mix, seasonality and other deploys; a control group served at the same time isolates the change.

flashcards.front: How do you protect an LLM feature from silent model changes?
flashcards.back: Pin model snapshot IDs rather than moving aliases, and run the regression suite on any candidate model before switching.

flashcards.front: Which token categories make up an LLM bill when prompt caching is used?
flashcards.back: Uncached input, cache writes (priced above base input), cache reads (priced far below base input) and output tokens (including reasoning tokens). Each has its own rate.

flashcards.front: On the Claude API, how do you get total input tokens from the usage block?
flashcards.back: Add input_tokens, cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens. input_tokens alone only counts tokens after the last cache breakpoint.

flashcards.front: In what order does Claude build the cacheable prefix?
flashcards.back: tools, then system, then messages. Changing tool definitions invalidates the whole cache; changing the system prompt invalidates system and messages.

flashcards.front: What happens to a prompt shorter than the model's minimum cacheable length?
flashcards.back: It is silently not cached: no error, just zero cache reads. The minimum varies by model.

flashcards.front: With a 1.25x write and 0.1x read multiplier, when does a 5-minute cache entry pay for itself?
flashcards.back: After a single cache hit: 1.25 + 0.1 is less than the 2.0 you would pay for two uncached requests.

flashcards.front: What do batch APIs trade, and what do they save?
flashcards.back: They trade latency (asynchronous, within a window of up to 24 hours) for about 50% off standard prices. On Claude the discount stacks with prompt caching.

flashcards.front: Why must batch results be joined on custom_id?
flashcards.back: Results can come back in any order, so position is meaningless. custom_id also lets you skip already completed work on a resubmit.

flashcards.front: What does streaming improve, and what does it not?
flashcards.back: It cuts perceived latency to roughly the time to first token. It does not shorten total generation time.

flashcards.front: On the Claude API, do cache reads count toward the input-tokens-per-minute limit?
flashcards.back: No. Default ITPM limits count only uncached input tokens, so a high cache hit rate raises effective throughput.

flashcards.front: Does a large max_tokens value use up Claude's output-tokens-per-minute limit?
flashcards.back: No. OTPM counts the tokens actually generated, not max_tokens.

flashcards.front: How do you recognise a 429 that retrying will not fix on the Claude API?
flashcards.back: The spend-cap 429 has no retry-after header and carries error_code "enforced_spend_limit_reached". Alert a human instead of retrying.

flashcards.front: Why add jitter to exponential backoff?
flashcards.back: Without jitter, clients that failed together retry together, in synchronized waves that keep the dependency overloaded. Random jitter spreads the retries out.

flashcards.front: What is an idempotency key?
flashcards.back: A caller-generated ID for one logical operation, sent with every attempt. The server stores the result under the key and returns it for repeats, so a retry after a timeout does not repeat the side effect.

flashcards.front: How should the OpenTelemetry GenAI inference span be named?
flashcards.back: "{gen_ai.operation.name} {gen_ai.request.model}", for example "chat claude-sonnet-5-5". The span is gen_ai.client.inference, kind CLIENT.

flashcards.front: Which OTel GenAI attribute identifies the model provider today?
flashcards.back: gen_ai.provider.name (required). It replaced the older gen_ai.system.

flashcards.front: Why are gen_ai.input.messages and gen_ai.output.messages opt-in?
flashcards.back: They are likely to contain sensitive user or PII data. Capture them deliberately, redacted or by reference with the *_ref variants.

flashcards.front: What is shadow traffic, and how does it differ from a canary?
flashcards.back: Shadow traffic copies real requests to a new version without showing its output to users. A canary serves the new version to a small share of real users.

flashcards.front: How does OpenAI now distinguish rate limiting from overload?
flashcards.back: Rate limiting returns 429 with slow_down; temporary overload returns 503 with server_is_overloaded. Honour Retry-After when it is provided.

flashcards.front: Direct vs indirect prompt injection
flashcards.back: Direct: the user types instructions to override the app. Indirect: instructions hidden in content the app reads (web pages, files, emails, tool results, retrieved chunks).

flashcards.front: Why can prompt injection not be fully filtered?
flashcards.back: Instructions and data share one token stream, so filters only guess at intent. OWASP LLM01: it is unclear if fool-proof prevention exists; RAG and fine-tuning do not fully mitigate it.

flashcards.front: OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025): LLM01 to LLM05
flashcards.back: LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure, LLM03 Supply Chain, LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning, LLM05 Improper Output Handling.

flashcards.front: OWASP LLM Top 10 (2025): LLM06 to LLM10
flashcards.back: LLM06 Excessive Agency, LLM07 System Prompt Leakage, LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, LLM09 Misinformation, LLM10 Unbounded Consumption.

flashcards.front: LLM05 Improper Output Handling: the core rule
flashcards.back: Treat model output as untrusted input to the next system: encode for HTML, parameterise SQL, never pass it raw to a shell or eval.

flashcards.front: LLM06 Excessive Agency: the fix
flashcards.back: Least privilege: only the tools the task needs, each with the narrowest scope, privileged checks in code, and human approval for high-risk actions.

flashcards.front: Where should untrusted content go in a Claude request?
flashcards.back: Only in tool results, with its source labelled; never in the system prompt or plain user text blocks. Do not put your own instructions in tool results.

flashcards.front: CaMeL in one sentence
flashcards.back: Derive the control and data flow from the trusted user query up front so untrusted data cannot change which steps run, and use capabilities on data to block exfiltration.

flashcards.front: Three common exfiltration channels for an injected agent
flashcards.back: URLs (fetched links or auto-rendered images carrying data in the query string), outbound tools (email, webhooks, HTTP), and writes to shared places others read.

flashcards.front: MCP: token passthrough rule
flashcards.back: MCP servers must validate that a token was issued for them (audience) and must not accept or pass through any other tokens; tokens go in the Authorization header, never the query string.

flashcards.front: MCP tool safety principle
flashcards.back: Tools represent arbitrary code execution: hosts must get explicit user consent before invoking any tool, and tool annotations are untrusted unless the server is trusted.

flashcards.front: Anthropic ZDR: what happens if a ZDR org calls Batch?
flashcards.back: The API does not block it; the request simply falls outside ZDR (Batch is not ZDR-eligible). HIPAA-enabled orgs get a 400 instead. Gate ineligible features in your code.

flashcards.front: OpenAI API data defaults
flashcards.back: Not used for training by default; abuse-monitoring logs kept up to 30 days; ZDR needs approval and forces store=false; Files, Conversations and vector stores are kept until deleted.

flashcards.front: OWASP LLM08 mitigations for multi-tenant RAG
flashcards.back: Permission-aware vector stores with strict partitioning, source validation and hidden-text extraction at ingestion, classification tags, and immutable retrieval logs.

flashcards.front: Anthropic harmlessness screen pattern
flashcards.back: A small fast model returns structured output like {is_harmful: boolean}; a refusal stop reason counts as harmful. Combine with input validation, bounded system prompt and throttling repeat offenders.

flashcards.front: How does a Claude refusal arrive?
flashcards.back: HTTP 200 with stop_reason "refusal" (billed); read stop_details and consider a fallback model. Branch on the field, not on status codes or text matching.

questions.scenario: Support chatbot
questions.stem: A support chatbot built on the Anthropic Messages API answers the first message well, but on the second turn it no longer knows the customer's order number. Each request sends the system prompt and only the latest user message. What is the fix?
options: Switch to a larger model with a bigger context window
Add "remember everything the customer said earlier" to the system prompt
Send the full prior list of `user` and `assistant` turns with every request
Raise `max_tokens` so the model can remember more
questions.explanation: The Messages API is stateless: the model only sees what is in the current request. The application must resend the prior turns each time. Instructions, output limits and bigger windows do not give the model history it was never sent.
rationales: A bigger window is useless if the history is never sent.
The model cannot recall turns that are not in the request, however it is instructed.
Correct. The client owns conversation state and must resend it.
`max_tokens` caps output length; it has nothing to do with history.

questions.scenario: Report summarizer
questions.stem: A nightly job summarizes long reports with Claude. About 3% of summaries end mid-sentence, and the job stores them as finished. Logs show `stop_reason: "max_tokens"` on exactly those responses. What should the job do?
options: Ignore `stop_reason` and check whether the last character is punctuation
Retry the identical request until the summary ends with a full stop
Add "keep the summary short" to the prompt and keep storing all responses
Treat `max_tokens` as truncated output: raise the output budget or split the task, and never store it as complete
questions.explanation: `max_tokens` means generation hit your output cap, so the text is truncated. The job should branch on that stop reason and fix the budget or task size. Identical retries and text heuristics do not address the cause.
rationales: Punctuation is a fragile proxy; `stop_reason` already says why it stopped.
The same request with the same budget is likely to truncate again.
May reduce frequency, but truncated outputs are still saved as complete.
Correct. Branch on the structured stop reason and fix the budget.

questions.scenario: Content pipeline
questions.stem: A moderation-adjacent pipeline sometimes gets HTTP 200 responses from Claude with `stop_reason: "refusal"`. The current code sees no error, tries to parse the text as the expected JSON, fails, and resends the identical request up to 10 times. What is the best change?
options: Search the response text for phrases like "I can't" and only then retry
Wrap the call in exponential backoff so the retries are spaced out
Lower the temperature to make refusals less likely
Branch on `refusal`: read `stop_details`, then retry on a fallback model or route the item to human review instead of resending unchanged
questions.explanation: A Claude refusal is a successful HTTP response with a distinct stop reason, and `stop_details` explains it. The stop-reasons guidance is to handle it explicitly, for example by retrying on a fallback model, not by looping on the same request. Sampling parameters are rejected on the current API version anyway.
rationales: Text matching is fragile when a structured stop reason exists.
Backoff is for transient capacity errors; it just spaces out identical refusals.
Sampling parameters are rejected on current Claude, and they are not a refusal control.
Correct. Refusal is a control-flow branch with its own handling.

questions.scenario: Research assistant
questions.stem: A research assistant uses a server-side web search tool. On complex questions the response ends with `stop_reason: "pause_turn"` and a partial answer, which the app currently shows to users as final. What should the app do?
options: Strip the partial content and send the original question again
Raise `max_tokens` because `pause_turn` means the output cap was hit
Show the partial answer and append "results may be incomplete"
Send the response content back unchanged in a follow-up request so the model can continue
questions.explanation: `pause_turn` means a server-tool loop hit its iteration limit (10 by default). The documented handling is to send the content back unchanged so the turn can continue. It is not an output-cap signal.
rationales: Discards the work done so far and will likely pause again.
That is `max_tokens`; `pause_turn` is about the server-tool iteration limit.
The turn is not finished, so the user gets an incomplete answer.
Correct. Resend the assistant content as-is to resume.

questions.scenario: Tool-using agent
questions.stem: After a tool call, an agent sends a user message containing the `tool_result` block followed by a text block, "Here is the result, continue." Claude often replies with `end_turn` and only 2 to 3 tokens. The team plans to auto-retry empty responses. What is the better fix?
options: Auto-retry the same request up to three times
Switch the agent to a larger model
Remove the text block placed right after the `tool_result` blocks, so the message holds only the tool results
Raise `max_tokens` so the model has room to answer
questions.explanation: The stop-reasons page traces empty `end_turn` responses to text blocks placed right after `tool_result` blocks, and says not to retry empty responses without modification. Fixing the message shape removes the cause. Budget and model size are unrelated.
rationales: The docs warn against retrying empty responses unchanged.
The cause is the request shape, not model capability.
Correct. Fix the message shape that causes the empty turn.
The model stopped by choice (`end_turn`), not because of the cap.

questions.scenario: Streaming chat UI
questions.stem: A chat UI streams Claude responses. To decide whether to show a "continue" button, the client reads `stop_reason` from the `message_start` event, and it is always null. Where should it read the stop reason?
options: From the first `content_block_start` event
Nowhere: stop reasons are not available when streaming
From the HTTP status code of the streaming response
From the `message_delta` event near the end of the stream
questions.explanation: In a Claude stream, `stop_reason` is null in `message_start` and arrives in `message_delta`, after the content blocks. Streaming does report it; it just arrives late. The HTTP status is 200 before any content is generated.
rationales: Content-block events carry content, not the final stop reason.
Stop reasons are reported in the stream.
The status is sent before generation ends, so it cannot say why it stopped.
Correct. `message_delta` carries the stop reason and cumulative usage.

questions.scenario: Streaming backend
questions.stem: You are hardening a backend that consumes Claude streaming responses and records the token usage. Which two behaviours must it handle? (Select two.)
options: Usage in `message_delta` is cumulative, so record the latest value rather than summing deltas
An error event such as `overloaded_error` can arrive mid-stream after the HTTP 200
A 200 status guarantees the full response will be delivered
The final `stop_reason` is always present in `message_start`
questions.explanation: A stream can fail after the 200 status, so the consumer must handle error events and partial content. Usage in `message_delta` is cumulative, and summing it double-counts. The stop reason arrives in `message_delta`, not `message_start`.
rationales: Correct. Summing cumulative usage overcounts tokens.
Correct. Mid-stream errors are possible after the 200.
The status is sent before generation; it cannot guarantee completion.
`stop_reason` is null in `message_start`.

questions.scenario: Provider migration
questions.stem: After moving to the OpenAI Responses API with a reasoning model, a service crashes intermittently. It reads the answer as `response.output[0].content[0].text`. What is the most robust fix?
options: Wrap the access in try/except and return an empty string on failure
Read `response.output[1]` instead, since reasoning comes first
Switch back to a non-reasoning model so `output[0]` is always the message
Use `response.output_text`, or iterate `output` and select items by type
questions.explanation: `output` is an array of typed items, and its order varies (reasoning items, tool calls, messages). The SDK's `output_text` helper, or selecting by type, is robust. Any fixed index will break again.
rationales: Hides the bug and returns empty answers.
Another fixed index that breaks when the item order changes.
Gives up capability to keep a brittle access pattern.
Correct. Select by type or use the helper.

questions.scenario: Healthcare startup
questions.stem: A team using the OpenAI Responses API must not let the provider retain response content beyond the request for its use case. What should they change first?
options: Send the content in a `developer` message instead of `user`
Delete the conversation from their own database after each session
Set `store: false` on requests, since responses are stored by default
Move the system rules into `instructions`
questions.explanation: Responses are stored for 30 days by default, and `store: false` turns that off. Where the guidance lives or which role it uses has no effect on retention, and local deletion does not affect the provider's copy.
rationales: Role choice does not affect storage.
Local deletion does not remove the provider-side stored response.
Correct. This disables default response storage.
`instructions` changes authority, not retention.

questions.scenario: Gemini assistant
questions.stem: A Gemini Interactions-based assistant sends `tools` and `system_instruction` on the first turn and then chains follow-ups using only `previous_interaction_id` and the new input. From turn 2 on, it stops calling tools and drops its persona. What is the cause?
options: `previous_interaction_id` expires after one turn
Gemini requires prefilling the model turn to keep the persona
The model's context window filled after one turn
`tools`, `system_instruction` and `generation_config` are interaction-scoped and must be re-sent on every turn
questions.explanation: With Interactions, the previous turn's content is chained, but tool definitions, system instructions and generation config apply only to the interaction that carries them. Re-sending them each turn restores the behaviour. Prefill returns a 400 on Gemini 3+.
rationales: The chain works; the model still sees the earlier conversation.
Prefill is rejected on current Gemini models.
One turn cannot fill a window of about 1M tokens.
Correct. These settings are per interaction.

questions.scenario: Data extraction service
questions.stem: An extraction service used to end each Claude request with an assistant turn containing `{` to force JSON. After moving to a current model, every request fails with a 400. What is the right replacement?
options: Write "RESPOND ONLY WITH JSON" in capitals in the system prompt
Move the `{` to the end of the user message
Pin the old API version so prefill keeps working
Use structured outputs (`output_config.format` with a JSON Schema) and validate the result
questions.explanation: Prefill is unsupported from Claude 4.6 on and returns a 400. Structured outputs constrain decoding to your schema, which is a stronger guarantee than prefill ever gave. Emphatic instructions still leave the format to chance.
rationales: Instructions alone do not guarantee schema-valid JSON.
A brace in the user turn does not constrain the reply.
Prefill is rejected by current models themselves, and pinning an old API version blocks upgrades without restoring it.
Correct. Use the schema-constrained feature built for this.

questions.scenario: Ticket classifier
questions.stem: A ticket classifier on Claude returns different labels for the same ticket across runs, and sometimes invents labels. An engineer proposes `temperature: 0`. On the current API version, what is the better approach?
options: Ask the model in the prompt to "use temperature zero"
Run each ticket three times and keep the longest answer
Set `top_p: 0` instead, since only temperature was removed
Constrain the label to a schema enum, add diverse labelled examples, and measure label agreement with repeated-trial evals
questions.explanation: The current Claude API version rejects `temperature`, `top_p` and `top_k` with a 400. An enum removes invented labels, examples steer the boundary cases, and repeated-trial evals measure consistency. Prompt text cannot change sampling.
rationales: The model cannot change its own decoding settings.
Longest is not a quality signal; majority voting at least targets agreement.
`top_p` is rejected as well.
Correct. Consistency comes from constraints, examples and measurement.

questions.scenario: Contract review
questions.stem: A contract-review prompt starts with the question, then pastes three 40-page contracts as plain text. Answers often mix up which contract a clause came from. Which restructuring best follows provider guidance?
options: Repeat the question after every contract
Move the contracts into the system prompt and leave the question in the user turn unchanged
Wrap each contract in its own tagged block with source metadata, put the contracts first, and put the question and instructions at the end
Summarize each contract to one paragraph before sending
questions.explanation: Both Anthropic and Google advise putting long material first and the query last, and Anthropic recommends tagging each document with metadata so the model can tell them apart. Summarizing first loses the clause-level detail the task needs.
rationales: Adds noise and does not separate the documents.
Moving untagged text around does not separate the contracts.
Correct. Tagged documents first, question last.
Destroys the detail needed for clause attribution.

questions.scenario: Email rewriter
questions.stem: A prompt includes four few-shot examples, all rewriting short complaints about late deliveries. In production the model mentions deliveries in emails about billing. What is the best fix?
options: Remove all examples and rely on the instruction alone
Add twenty more delivery examples to strengthen the pattern
Add "do not mention deliveries" to the instruction
Replace them with 3 to 5 diverse examples covering different topics and lengths, each wrapped in `<example>` tags
questions.explanation: Examples that share an incidental detail teach that detail. Anthropic advises 3 to 5 diverse examples in `<example>` tags so the model learns the pattern, not the topic. Removing examples loses format control, and patching one symptom leaves the bias in place.
rationales: Examples are among the most reliable controls; Google advises always including them.
More of the same strengthens the unwanted pattern.
Fixes one symptom; the examples still bias the output.
Correct. Diversity stops the model copying surface features.

questions.scenario: Reasoning audit
questions.stem: On a current Claude model with thinking always on, a team asks the model to "write your step-by-step reasoning inside <thinking> tags" so they can parse it, and some requests now end in a `reasoning_extraction` refusal. What should they do?
options: Prefill `<thinking>` in the assistant turn
Set `thinking: {type: "enabled", budget_tokens: 8000}` to control the reasoning manually
Repeat the instruction more firmly in the system prompt
Drop the tagged-reasoning request, rely on built-in thinking, and adjust `output_config.effort`; ask for a brief rationale field in the output if one is needed
questions.explanation: Manual chain of thought is a fallback for when thinking is off. On current models, asking for tagged reasoning can trigger a `reasoning_extraction` refusal, and manual `budget_tokens` thinking is not accepted on later models. Built-in thinking with an effort setting is the supported control.
rationales: Prefill returns a 400 on current Claude.
Manual budget thinking is not accepted on later models.
More insistence makes the refusal more likely, not less.
Correct. Use the built-in mechanism and request only what you need in the output.

questions.scenario: Autocomplete feature
questions.stem: An autocomplete feature runs on a Claude model where thinking is always on, and p95 latency is too high. Quality is more than adequate. What is the first lever to try without changing the model?
options: Disable thinking with `budget_tokens: 0`
Set `temperature` lower to speed decoding
Set `max_tokens` to 5 so responses are cut short
Lower `output_config.effort`
questions.explanation: Effort controls how much the model thinks, which directly trades quality against latency and cost. Sampling parameters are rejected on the current API, a tiny output cap truncates answers, and manual budget thinking is not accepted on later models.
rationales: Manual budget thinking is not accepted on later models.
Rejected on the current API, and not a speed control.
Truncates answers rather than making the model think less.
Correct. Effort is the documented latency/quality dial.

questions.scenario: Lead enrichment
questions.stem: A service uses OpenAI JSON mode (`json_object`). Responses always parse, but some lack the `company_size` field and others use unexpected enum values. What change addresses the cause?
options: Retry until the response contains every field
Parse with a more lenient JSON parser
Add the field list to the prompt in bold
Switch to structured outputs with a `json_schema` format and `strict: true`
questions.explanation: JSON mode guarantees valid JSON, not schema adherence. Strict structured outputs constrain the output to your schema, including required fields and enums. Prompts and retries leave conformance to chance.
rationales: Blind retries cost money and still may not conform.
The JSON already parses; the problem is the schema.
Instructions improve the odds but guarantee nothing.
Correct. Schema-constrained decoding enforces fields and enums.

questions.scenario: Profile extraction
questions.stem: An OpenAI strict structured-output schema for a user profile has an optional `nickname` field, and the API rejects the schema. Which two changes are needed for strict mode? (Select two.)
options: List every property, including `nickname`, in `required` and make `nickname` a union of `string` and `null`
Set `additionalProperties: false` on every object in the schema
Remove `nickname` from `required` and add a default value
Combine the profile parts with `allOf`
questions.explanation: In strict mode every field must be in `required`, with optional fields written as a `null` union, and every object must set `additionalProperties: false`. Leaving a field out of `required` is how ordinary JSON Schema does it, but strict mode rejects it, and `allOf` is not supported.
rationales: Correct. Optional means nullable, not absent.
Correct. Required on every object in strict mode.
This is the pattern strict mode rejects.
`allOf` is unsupported in strict mode.

questions.scenario: Pricing extractor
questions.stem: A team ports a schema to Claude structured outputs. It uses `minimum`/`maximum` on `discount_percent` and `maxLength: 280` on `summary`. What is the most robust design?
options: Model `summary` as a recursive schema of shorter strings
Keep the constraints in the schema; constrained decoding will enforce them
Replace the schema with JSON mode and ask for the limits in the prompt
Remove the unsupported keywords from the schema sent to Claude and enforce the range and length in a Pydantic validator, with a repair retry on failure
questions.explanation: Anthropic structured outputs do not support numeric bounds or string-length keywords, nor recursive schemas. Keep the schema to supported keywords and enforce the extra rules in your own validator, retrying with the error if needed. Prompt-only limits are not enforced.
rationales: Recursive schemas are unsupported too.
These keywords are unsupported, so they will not be enforced.
Loses the schema guarantee you do have.
Correct. Portable schema plus application-side validation.

questions.scenario: Product catalogue
questions.stem: A Gemini structured-output schema sets `maxLength: 60` on product titles, yet some titles come back with 90 characters. The request succeeded without warnings. What explains this, and what should the team do?
options: The model hit its output cap; raise `max_output_tokens`
Length limits need `anyOf`; rewrite the field with `anyOf`
Gemini ignores the whole schema when it contains any string constraint; drop the schema
Gemini silently strips `maxLength` (and similar keywords); enforce the length in application validation
questions.explanation: Gemini drops `minLength`, `maxLength` and some other keywords without error, so they are not enforced, while the rest of the schema still applies. The fix is to validate lengths in app code. Truncation would make titles shorter, not longer.
rationales: A cap would shorten output, not lengthen it.
`anyOf` is supported but does not enforce length.
The rest of the schema is still enforced; only some keywords are stripped.
Correct. Silent stripping means you must validate yourself.

questions.scenario: Claims intake
questions.stem: A claims-intake pipeline validates every model response with a Pydantic model. Which two repair behaviours are sound? (Select two.)
options: On a `ValidationError` for complete output, retry once with the validation error message added to the prompt, then escalate
Fill any missing fields with default values so the pipeline never fails
On a refusal or truncation stop reason, branch on that signal (fallback model, larger budget or review) instead of retrying the same request
Retry unchanged until validation passes
questions.explanation: Failures have different causes and need different repairs. Feeding the validation error back gives the model a precise correction target; refusals and truncation are signalled by the stop reason and need a different path. Blind retries waste money, and silent defaults turn visible failures into wrong data.
rationales: Correct. A targeted, capped repair retry.
Hides failures as plausible-looking wrong data.
Correct. Branch on the cause signalled by the API.
Unbounded identical retries rarely fix the cause.

questions.scenario: Triage router
questions.stem: A triage router uses Claude structured outputs with a `priority` enum of `high`, `medium` and `low`. Downstream code uses an exact-match switch, and a small number of items fall through because `priority` arrived as `High`. What is the most appropriate fix?
options: Drop structured outputs and parse free text
Add a fourth enum value `High`
Retry the request whenever the casing differs
Normalize or compare the enum value case-insensitively during validation before routing
questions.explanation: Anthropic's structured-outputs page notes that enum casing can differ and advises case-insensitive comparison. Normalizing during validation fixes this cheaply. The other options either lose the schema benefit or treat a cosmetic difference as a failure.
rationales: Throws away the schema guarantee for a casing issue.
Proliferates near-duplicate values and does not cover other casings.
Pays for retries over a difference you can normalize.
Correct. Normalize in the validation layer.

questions.scenario: Multi-schema extractor
questions.stem: An extractor sends a long, stable system prompt with prompt caching, but picks one of eight slightly different JSON schemas per request via `output_config.format`. The cache hit rate is far lower than expected. What is the likely cause and fix?
options: The system prompt is too long to cache; shorten it
Structured outputs disable caching entirely; remove caching
Cached prefixes expire after each request when schemas are used
Changing `output_config.format` invalidates the prompt cache; consolidate to one stable schema or group requests by schema
questions.explanation: Anthropic documents that changing `output_config.format` invalidates the prompt cache, so rotating schemas keeps breaking it. A single stable schema (or batching requests by schema) lets the cached prefix be reused. Long prompts are what caching is for.
rationales: Long stable prefixes are the best case for caching.
Caching works with structured outputs when the format is stable.
The cause is the format change, not a per-request expiry.
Correct. Keep the format stable to keep cache hits.

questions.scenario: Cost forecasting
questions.stem: A team forecasts Claude spend by converting word counts to tokens with a ratio measured on an older Claude generation. After upgrading to a current model, actual input tokens are noticeably higher. What should they change?
options: Remove whitespace from prompts to reduce token counts
Nothing; the provider is overbilling
Use four characters per token as the universal ratio
Count tokens for the target model with the provider's token counter (and track `usage`) instead of a fixed word ratio
questions.explanation: Anthropic states its current tokenizer fits about 555k words in 1M tokens, versus about 750k on earlier models, so the same text uses more tokens. Counting with the target model and reading `usage` gives accurate budgets. Any fixed ratio drifts when the tokenizer changes.
rationales: Micro-optimization that misses the cause.
The tokenizer change explains the increase.
A rough heuristic, not a forecast basis.
Correct. Measure with the model you will use.

questions.scenario: Policy Q&A agent
questions.stem: A policy Q&A agent has a 1M-token window, so the team now puts all 300 retrieved policy sections into every prompt instead of the top 10. Accuracy drops, especially when the answer sits in sections in the middle of the list. What is the best response?
options: Repeat each section twice to raise its weight
Move the question to the middle of the context so it is near more sections
Return to a small, high-signal set (for example reranked top sections), and place the most relevant material at the start or end
Keep all 300 sections; larger windows recall everything equally
questions.explanation: Context rot means recall falls as context grows, and "Lost in the Middle" shows the middle of a long input is recalled worst. The fix is to curate the smallest high-signal context and position key material well. Filling the window adds noise and cost.
rationales: Doubles tokens and noise without fixing selection.
Middle positions are the weakest place for key content.
Correct. Curate and position for attention.
Recall degrades with length; the window size is not a recall guarantee.
