questions.scenario: Internal handbook bot
questions.stem: An internal handbook of about 120,000 tokens (around 300 pages) changes a few times a year. The team plans to build chunking, embeddings and a vector store for a Q&A bot. What is the simplest design worth evaluating first?
options: Fine-tune a model on the handbook
Build the full RAG pipeline; long context never works
Split the handbook across ten parallel requests and merge the answers
Put the whole handbook in the prompt, with prompt caching for the repeated prefix
questions.explanation: Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval post says a knowledge base under 200,000 tokens can go straight into the prompt, and caching makes the repeated prefix cheap. Measure that baseline before taking on a retrieval pipeline. Fine-tuning is a poor way to inject facts that change.
rationales: Costly and poor at keeping facts current.
Overbuilds for a corpus that fits in the window.
Adds merge complexity and loses cross-section reasoning.
Correct. A small, stable corpus fits in context.

questions.scenario: Gemini analyst
questions.stem: After raising the thinking level on a Gemini model, a report generator starts returning truncated answers, and output-token costs rise. `max_output_tokens` is unchanged. What explains both effects?
options: Thinking tokens are free but slow, causing time-outs
Higher thinking levels shrink the context window
Thinking tokens count toward `max_output_tokens` and are billed as output
The thinking level resets the system instruction
questions.explanation: On Gemini, thinking tokens are billed as output and are included in `max_output_tokens`. More thinking leaves less room for the visible answer and costs more. Raise the output cap or lower the thinking level.
rationales: Thinking tokens are billed as output.
The window size does not change with thinking level.
Correct. Thinking shares the output budget and price.
Unrelated to truncation or cost.

questions.scenario: High-volume classifier
questions.stem: A team sends 5 million short ticket-classification requests a day to the provider's top-capability model "to be safe". Costs are far over budget. What should they do first?
options: Ask the provider for a discount and change nothing
Shorten the system prompt by half
Move all traffic to the smallest model immediately
Run their eval set on cheaper tiers (and lower effort settings), then route classification to the cheapest option that meets the quality bar
questions.explanation: Model choice should come from measured quality on your own evals against cost and latency. Short classification is usually well served by smaller tiers, but switching without measuring risks silent quality loss. Prompt trimming helps far less than the per-token price gap between tiers.
rationales: Does not address the mismatch between task and model.
Small savings compared with tier pricing differences.
Right direction, but unmeasured; quality could drop silently.
Correct. Measure, then route by task.

questions.scenario: Code review assistant
questions.stem: A code-review assistant on Anthropic's recommended general model is slightly below the team's quality bar on hard cases. Before moving everything to the top-priced tier, what does Anthropic's guidance suggest trying?
options: Add prefill to steer the review format
Increase `max_tokens` to the model maximum
Raise `temperature` for more creative reviews
Raise the effort setting and re-run the evals
questions.explanation: Anthropic's choosing-a-model page notes that tuning effort is often a better lever than switching models. Measure the result on the same evals. Sampling parameters and prefill are rejected on current Claude, and a larger cap alone does not make the model reason more.
rationales: Prefill returns a 400 on current models.
The cap limits length; it does not improve reasoning.
Rejected on the current API.
Correct. Effort first, measured by evals.

questions.scenario: Regulated workflow
questions.stem: A regulated workflow must not change behaviour without review, yet the team wants to adopt better models over time. Which practice fits?
options: Pin the exact snapshot model ID, track deprecation dates, and rerun the eval suite before switching IDs
Let each developer pick a model at runtime
Avoid upgrades entirely to keep behaviour fixed
Use an alias that always points to the newest model
questions.explanation: Claude model IDs are pinned snapshots, and older models retire on published dates. Pinning plus eval-gated upgrades gives stable behaviour and a controlled path to newer models. Never upgrading eventually hits a retirement.
rationales: Correct. Pin, monitor deprecations, gate with evals.
Uncontrolled variation is the opposite of the requirement.
Retirements will force a change anyway, unplanned.
Behaviour can change without review.

questions.scenario: Cross-provider fallback
questions.stem: You add an OpenAI fallback behind a Claude-first extraction service. Which two things must the adapter layer handle for the fallback to be safe? (Select two.)
options: Validate both providers' outputs with the same Pydantic model, because each provider supports a different JSON Schema subset
Map refusal and truncation signals: Claude uses `stop_reason` values, while OpenAI returns a `refusal` content part and `status: "incomplete"`
Copy the Claude request body unchanged to the OpenAI endpoint
Reuse Claude token counts to budget OpenAI requests, since tokenizers match
questions.explanation: The providers signal refusals and truncation differently and enforce different schema subsets, so the adapter must translate failure signals and validate outputs identically. Tokenizers and request shapes differ, so copying counts or bodies across will break.
rationales: Correct. One validator is the common contract.
Correct. Failure signals differ by provider.
Request shapes and field names differ.
Tokenizers differ across providers.

questions.scenario: Overnight batch
questions.stem: An overnight job retries every Claude 429 with exponential backoff. One night every request fails until morning. The 429 responses have no `retry-after` header and carry `error.details.error_code: "enforced_spend_limit_reached"`. What should the client have done?
options: Switched to streaming to bypass rate limits
Retried faster to finish before the limit reset
Lowered `max_tokens`, since OTPM limits count the requested maximum
Treated it as a spend cap: stop retrying, alert an operator, and fail over or pause the job
questions.explanation: A spend-cap 429 has no `retry-after`, and retries keep failing until the cap changes. The client should recognise the error code and stop. OTPM counts actual tokens, so `max_tokens` is not the issue, and streaming does not bypass limits.
rationales: Streaming does not change rate or spend limits.
Retries cannot succeed while the cap is in force.
OTPM counts actual output, not `max_tokens`.
Correct. Distinguish spend caps from transient limits.

questions.scenario: A finance assistant indexes quarterly reports in 300-token chunks. Users ask 'What was ACME's revenue growth in Q2 2023?', and the retriever keeps returning chunks such as 'Revenue grew 3% over the previous quarter' from the wrong companies' reports.
questions.stem: Which change most directly addresses the root cause?
options: Before indexing, prepend to each chunk a short LLM-generated context that situates it in its document (company, period), then embed and BM25-index the contextualized chunk.
Switch to an embedding model with more dimensions.
Add a system-prompt instruction telling the model to ignore chunks from other companies.
Raise top-k from 5 to 50 so the right chunk is more likely to be included.
questions.explanation: The chunks have lost the context that identifies which company and quarter they describe, so no query can distinguish them. Contextual Retrieval fixes this by prepending document-aware context to each chunk before embedding and before building the BM25 index. Anthropic reports this cut top-20 retrieval failures by 35% for embeddings alone and 49% together with contextual BM25.
rationales: Correct. It restores the missing context in both the embedding and the lexical index.
More dimensions cannot encode information that is not in the chunk text.
The model cannot reliably tell which company a context-free chunk belongs to, so a prompt instruction does not fix retrieval.
A larger k adds more look-alike chunks and prompt cost; it does not make the right chunk distinguishable.

questions.scenario: An internal HR assistant answers questions from a single policy handbook of about 120 pages (roughly 90,000 tokens). It changes twice a year. The team is about to build chunking, an embedding pipeline and a vector database.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate first approach?
options: Fine-tune a model on the handbook so answers come from its weights.
Build the full RAG pipeline with hybrid search and reranking from day one.
Put the whole handbook in the prompt and use prompt caching, and evaluate before adding retrieval.
Summarize the handbook into 2 pages and put only the summary in the prompt.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval post notes that a knowledge base under about 200,000 tokens can simply be included in the prompt, and prompt caching makes repeated use cheaper and faster. A 90,000-token handbook fits comfortably, so a retrieval layer adds complexity without a demonstrated benefit. Measure answer quality first and add RAG only if needed.
rationales: Fine-tuning is a poor way to inject facts that must be cited and updated.
This may work, but it is unnecessary engineering for a corpus that fits in context.
Correct. The corpus is under the roughly 200K-token threshold and is stable enough to cache.
A 2-page summary discards the policy detail employees ask about.

questions.scenario: A product team wants its support bot to answer from release notes and knowledge-base articles that change every week. Answers must link to the source article. One engineer proposes fine-tuning on the articles monthly.
questions.stem: Why is retrieval-augmented generation the better fit here?
options: Fine-tuning is unavailable from all major providers.
Fine-tuned models cannot follow a system prompt.
Retrieved documents form an updatable, inspectable memory, so new articles are searchable as soon as they are indexed and answers can cite them.
RAG removes hallucination completely because the model only copies text.
questions.explanation: The RAG paper's motivation is that non-parametric memory can be updated and inspected, unlike knowledge stored in the weights. Weekly changes and a citation requirement both favour retrieval. Fine-tuning would lag behind each update and cannot point to a source document.
rationales: This overstates the situation; availability varies by provider and is not the design reason.
Fine-tuned models still follow system prompts; this is not the reason.
Correct. Indexing a new article makes it available immediately and gives a citable source.
RAG reduces but does not eliminate hallucination; the model can still misread or ignore context.

questions.scenario: A SaaS company runs one shared vector index for all customers. The prompt says 'Only use documents belonging to tenant {id}.' A security review finds that answers sometimes quote another customer's documents.
questions.stem: What is the correct fix?
options: Enforce tenant isolation in retrieval, with a mandatory tenant filter or per-tenant partitions, so other tenants' chunks never reach the prompt.
Encrypt the embeddings at rest.
Strengthen the prompt with capital letters and repeat the tenant rule at the end.
Ask the model to output the tenant ID of each cited chunk and drop answers that mismatch.
questions.explanation: OWASP LLM08 lists cross-context leaks in multi-tenant vector databases as a risk and recommends permission-aware vector stores with strict partitioning. Prompt instructions are not an access control, because the model has already seen the other tenant's text. Filtering at retrieval time guarantees the data is never exposed.
rationales: Correct. Access control belongs in the retrieval query or the data layout.
Encryption at rest protects storage; it does nothing about what retrieval returns at query time.
Prompt wording cannot guarantee isolation once foreign data is in context.
Post-hoc checks rely on the model reporting honestly and still expose the data to it.

sources.title: LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses — OWASP GenAI

questions.scenario: You are designing the chunk schema for a RAG system that must cite sources, support re-indexing when documents change, and serve multiple customers.
questions.stem: Which TWO fields are most important to store with every chunk? (Select two.)
options: The source document ID and version.
The tenant or permission tags used to filter retrieval.
The model's last generated answer that used this chunk.
The raw embedding of the user's most recent query.
questions.explanation: A source ID and version let you cite the document, deduplicate, and find and replace stale chunks when a document changes. Tenant and permission tags let retrieval enforce access control, which OWASP LLM08 recommends through permission-aware stores and classification tags. Generated answers and query vectors are per-request data, not chunk metadata.
rationales: Correct. Needed for citations and for re-indexing changed documents.
Correct. Needed to filter retrieval by tenant or permission.
Storing answers on chunks couples the index to transient output and can leak data between users.
Query embeddings belong to the request, not to the stored chunk.

sources.title: LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses — OWASP GenAI

questions.scenario: A RAG pipeline passes 40 retrieved chunks, about 30,000 tokens, to the model in retrieval order. Evaluation shows the model often misses facts that the labelled set says are present in chunks 15–25.
questions.stem: Which change is most consistent with the published evidence on long-context behaviour?
options: Shuffle the chunk order randomly on each request.
Add more chunks so the missed facts appear more than once.
Pass fewer, better-ranked chunks (for example, by reranking) and keep the most relevant ones at the start or end of the context.
Lower the sampling temperature so the model reads more carefully.
questions.explanation: 'Lost in the Middle' found U-shaped performance: models use information at the beginning or end of a long context best and the middle worst. Anthropic's context-engineering guidance treats context as a finite attention budget, so trimming to fewer, better-ranked chunks also helps. Reranking and position-aware ordering address both.
rationales: Random order does not keep relevant chunks out of the middle.
More context deepens the middle and spends more of the attention budget.
Correct. Fewer, better-ranked chunks placed where models attend best.
Temperature does not change how the model attends to position, and current models may ignore or reject sampling parameters.

sources.title: Lost in the Middle — arXiv (Liu et al.)

questions.scenario: To cut costs, a team switched its embedding model. New documents are embedded with the new model; the two million existing vectors from the old model stay in the same index. Queries are embedded with the new model. Recall on old documents collapsed.
questions.stem: What is the cause and fix?
options: Old vectors must be re-normalized to length 1.
The HNSW index is corrupted; run REINDEX.
Vectors from different embedding models are not comparable; re-embed the existing corpus with the new model (ideally into a parallel index) and switch over after evaluation.
The new model needs a higher `hnsw.ef_search`; raise it to 400.
questions.explanation: Each embedding model defines its own vector space, so similarity between a new-model query and old-model documents is meaningless. The fix is to re-embed the whole corpus with the new model, typically building a second index, comparing on a labelled set, and cutting over. Storing the model ID with each vector makes such mixing detectable.
rationales: Normalization does not map one model's space onto another's.
Rebuilding the index keeps the same incompatible vectors.
Correct. Changing the model requires re-embedding everything.
A larger search beam cannot fix vectors that live in different spaces.

questions.scenario: Your corpus is embedded with OpenAI embeddings, which are normalized to length 1, and stored in pgvector. A teammate asks whether to use cosine distance, L2 distance or inner product for the HNSW index.
questions.stem: What is the best guidance?
options: Use cosine only; inner product is undefined for normalized vectors.
Use Hamming distance for speed.
Use L2; cosine gives a different ranking for normalized vectors.
All three give the same ranking for unit vectors; prefer inner product, which pgvector recommends for best performance with normalized vectors.
questions.explanation: For unit-length vectors, cosine similarity equals the dot product, and cosine and Euclidean distance produce the same ranking, as OpenAI's embeddings guide notes. pgvector's README says to use inner product for best performance when vectors are normalized. The choice is then about speed, not quality.
rationales: Inner product is perfectly defined and equals cosine for unit vectors.
Hamming distance applies to binary `bit` vectors, not float embeddings.
For normalized vectors, cosine and L2 rank identically.
Correct. Same ranking; inner product is the fastest choice.

questions.scenario: A team uses an embedding model that returns 3072-dimension vectors and stores them in a pgvector `vector(3072)` column. `CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw` fails because the column has too many dimensions for the index.
questions.stem: Which approach fixes this while keeping approximate nearest-neighbour search?
options: Raise the HNSW `m` parameter so the graph can handle more dimensions.
Switch the index type to IVFFlat.
Split each vector into two 1536-value halves in separate columns and index each half independently.
Request shorter embeddings (for example, 1536) with the API's `dimensions` parameter, re-embed the corpus and index the shorter column.
questions.explanation: At the time of writing, pgvector indexes `vector` columns only up to 2,000 dimensions with both HNSW and IVFFlat (`halfvec` raises this to 4,000). OpenAI's `dimensions` parameter returns shorter vectors that remain usable because the leading dimensions carry the representation. Re-embedding at a supported size restores indexing; switching to `halfvec` would be the other valid route.
rationales: `m` controls graph connectivity, not the dimension limit.
IVFFlat has the same 2,000-dimension limit for `vector`.
Searching two halves independently does not compute the true similarity of the full vectors.
Correct. Shorter vectors fit the index limit and keep good quality.

questions.scenario: To save storage, an engineer keeps only the first 256 values of each stored embedding. The service still ranks by dot product, assuming it equals cosine similarity. Ranking quality drops more than expected, and the dot-product order no longer matches a cosine-similarity check.
questions.stem: What went wrong?
options: Truncated vectors are no longer unit length, so dot product no longer equals cosine; they must be re-normalized (or shortened via the API's `dimensions` parameter).
Embeddings cannot be shortened at all; the full vector must always be used.
Dot product only works on vectors with more than 1,000 dimensions.
The index needs `ef_construction` raised to match the new dimension.
questions.explanation: OpenAI's guide notes that its embeddings are normalized to length 1, and that if you shorten them yourself you must re-normalize. Cutting off values reduces the vector's length, so dot product stops being equal to cosine and rankings diverge. Re-normalizing, or requesting short vectors with `dimensions`, restores the equivalence.
rationales: Correct. Truncation breaks unit length; re-normalize.
Shortening is supported and works well for models trained for it.
Dot product works at any dimension.
Build parameters do not fix vectors that are no longer normalized.

questions.stem: Why can the leading dimensions of some embedding models be used on their own as a smaller embedding?
options: Cosine similarity ignores all but the first dimensions.
Vector databases automatically compress trailing dimensions.
The models are trained, as in Matryoshka Representation Learning, so that nested prefixes of the vector are themselves useful representations.
Trailing dimensions are always zero padding.
questions.explanation: Matryoshka Representation Learning trains a single embedding so that its leading dimensions form usable representations at several sizes. The paper reports up to 14 times smaller embeddings at the same ImageNet accuracy. Models trained this way can be shortened with little quality loss.
rationales: Cosine similarity uses all dimensions equally.
Databases do not compress dimensions in a way that preserves meaning.
Correct. Nested, prefix-usable representations come from how the model is trained.
Trailing dimensions carry real information, just less of it.

questions.scenario: A developer queries pgvector with `SELECT id, embedding <#> $1 AS score FROM chunks ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 5` on normalized vectors. The results are consistently the least relevant chunks.
questions.stem: What is the bug?
options: Inner product cannot be used with an HNSW index.
The LIMIT clause is applied before ordering.
`<#>` is L1 distance; use `<+>` instead.
`<#>` returns the negative inner product, so ordering descending returns the least similar rows; order ascending and multiply by −1 to display similarity.
questions.explanation: pgvector's `<#>` operator returns the negative inner product, so that smaller values mean more similar, consistent with the other distance operators. Sorting descending therefore returns the worst matches. Use `ORDER BY embedding <#> $1` ascending and multiply by −1 if you need the similarity score.
rationales: pgvector supports HNSW with inner-product operator classes.
SQL applies LIMIT after ORDER BY.
`<+>` is L1 distance; `<#>` is negative inner product.
Correct. The sign convention flips the meaning of descending order.

questions.scenario: A pgvector HNSW query with `WHERE category = 'billing' ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 10` often returns only 3 or 4 rows. About 10% of rows have that category, and the index uses default settings.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes address this? (Select two.)
options: Enable iterative index scans (`SET hnsw.iterative_scan = relaxed_order` or `strict_order`) so more of the index is scanned when filtered rows run short.
Lower `hnsw.ef_search` to 10 to make the scan faster.
Use a partial HNSW index for `category = 'billing'` (or partition by category), so the index only contains matching rows.
Switch the operator to `<#>` because cosine distance is incompatible with WHERE clauses.
questions.explanation: pgvector applies filters after an approximate index scan; with the default `ef_search` of 40 and a 10% filter, about 4 matching rows survive on average. Iterative index scans automatically scan more of the index when needed. A partial index (for a few values) or partitioning (for many) makes the index contain only matching rows.
rationales: Correct. Iterative scans keep scanning until enough filtered rows are found or a cap is hit.
A smaller candidate list leaves even fewer rows after filtering.
Correct. A partial index or partition matches the filter, so nothing is discarded after the scan.
Every distance operator works with WHERE; the operator is not the problem.

questions.scenario: An HNSW index in pgvector was built with default parameters. Latency is well within budget, but recall@10 against exact search is lower than the team wants.
questions.stem: What is the first parameter to adjust?
options: Increase `hnsw.ef_search`, the query-time candidate list size, and re-measure recall and latency.
Decrease `m` to 4.
Switch to IVFFlat with `probes` = 1.
Shorten the vectors to 64 dimensions.
questions.explanation: `hnsw.ef_search` (default 40) sets the size of the dynamic candidate list at query time; a larger value explores more of the graph, giving higher recall at higher latency. It can be changed per session without rebuilding. Since latency has headroom, it is the cheapest lever to pull first.
rationales: Correct. More candidates explored means better recall, at a latency cost you can afford.
Fewer connections per node lowers recall.
IVFFlat with a single probe usually has worse recall.
Aggressive shortening usually lowers quality, not raises it.

questions.scenario: A team created an IVFFlat index on a new, empty `chunks` table, then bulk-loaded 2 million vectors. Recall is poor even after raising `ivfflat.probes`.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause?
options: The vectors must be stored as `bit` for IVFFlat.
IVFFlat cannot hold more than 1 million rows.
The index's cluster centres were computed when the table had no data; IVFFlat should be built after loading data.
`probes` must equal `m`.
questions.explanation: IVFFlat partitions vectors into lists whose centres are learned from the rows present at build time. pgvector's README says to create the index after the table has data. Building it on an empty table yields useless clusters; rebuild it after loading, sizing `lists` at about rows/1000 up to 1M rows and sqrt(rows) beyond.
rationales: IVFFlat supports `vector` and `halfvec` columns.
There is no such row limit; the README gives sizing guidance for larger tables.
Correct. Clusters learned from no data cannot partition the vectors well.
`m` is an HNSW parameter, unrelated to IVFFlat probes.

questions.scenario: Support engineers search a developer-docs RAG system with queries like 'ERR_TLS_CERT_ALTNAME_INVALID' or 'SKU 8841-B'. Dense retrieval returns topically similar but wrong pages, while conceptual questions work well.
questions.stem: What is the best improvement?
options: Lowercase all queries before embedding.
Increase chunk size so each chunk contains more identifiers.
Use a larger embedding model.
Add a BM25 lexical index and run hybrid search, fusing the lexical and dense results.
questions.explanation: Exact identifiers carry little semantic signal, so dense embeddings retrieve near neighbours in meaning rather than exact matches. BM25 excels at exact lexical matches, and Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval post motivates BM25 with exactly this error-code case. Hybrid search keeps dense retrieval's strength on conceptual queries.
rationales: Lowercasing does not make embeddings match exact strings.
Larger chunks dilute embeddings and do not fix exact matching.
A bigger model still represents identifiers by meaning, not exact strings.
Correct. Lexical matching catches identifiers; fusion keeps semantic recall.

sources.title: BEIR retrieval benchmark — arXiv (Thakur et al.)

questions.scenario: Hybrid search fuses a BM25 list and a dense list with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, RRF(d) = Σ 1/(k + rank), k = 60. Document A is ranked 1st in BM25 and 3rd in dense. Document B is 2nd in both. Document C is 1st in dense and absent from BM25.
questions.stem: What is the fused order?
options: B, A, C
A, C, B
A, B, C
C, A, B
questions.explanation: A scores 1/61 + 1/63 ≈ 0.032266, B scores 2/62 ≈ 0.032258, and C scores only 1/61 ≈ 0.016393. A narrowly beats B, and C trails because it appears in only one list. RRF rewards consistent presence across lists more than topping a single one.
rationales: C scores about half of B, so it cannot rank above B.
C has the lowest score because it appears in only one list.

sources.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion — Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher (SIGIR 2009)

questions.scenario: An engineer merges hybrid results by adding each document's cosine similarity (0 to 1) to its BM25 score (often 5 to 30). The final order is almost identical to BM25 alone.
questions.stem: What is the better approach?
options: Multiply cosine similarity by 100 before adding.
Take the maximum of the two raw scores.
Drop BM25 since it dominates.
Fuse by rank using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (or rerank the union with a cross-encoder), which needs no score calibration.
questions.explanation: Raw BM25 and cosine scores are on incompatible, query-dependent scales, so summing them lets BM25 dominate. RRF uses only each document's rank in each list, so no calibration is needed. pgvector's README suggests combining hybrid results with Reciprocal Rank Fusion or a cross-encoder.
rationales: A fixed multiplier is brittle because BM25's range varies by query and corpus.
Max of raw scores has the same scale problem.
Dropping BM25 loses exact-match recall.
Correct. Rank-based fusion avoids the scale mismatch.

sources.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion — Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher (SIGIR 2009)

questions.stem: In Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval experiments, which THREE techniques combined gave the lowest top-20 retrieval failure rate (1 − recall@20)? (Select three.)
options: Contextual Embeddings (embedding chunks with prepended, LLM-generated context).
Contextual BM25 (building the BM25 index over the contextualized chunks).
Reranking a larger candidate set before passing the top 20.
Fine-tuning the embedding model on the corpus.
questions.explanation: The post reports a 5.7% baseline failure rate, 3.7% with contextual embeddings, 2.9% after adding contextual BM25, and 1.9% after adding reranking, a 67% reduction overall. Fine-tuning the embedding model was not part of the method.
rationales: Correct. Alone it gave a 35% reduction.
Correct. Combined with contextual embeddings it gave a 49% reduction.
Correct. Adding reranking brought the reduction to 67%.
Not part of the method; the gains came from context, hybrid search and reranking.

questions.scenario: A pipeline retrieves the top 10 chunks by hybrid search, reranks them with a cross-encoder, and passes the top 5 to the model. Adding the reranker barely improved recall@5 against the labelled set, which shows that relevant chunks often rank 30th to 100th in the first stage.
questions.stem: What change would most improve results?
options: Remove the reranker since it does not help.
Pass all 10 first-stage chunks to the model unchanged.
Replace the cross-encoder with a larger one.
Retrieve a much larger candidate set (for example, the top 150) for the reranker, then pass its top results to the model.
questions.explanation: A reranker can only reorder the candidates it receives, so relevant chunks ranked 30th to 100th never reach it. Contextual Retrieval retrieves the top 150, reranks, and passes the top 20. Widening the candidate set lets the reranker's precision lift those chunks into the final set.
rationales: The reranker is not the bottleneck; the candidate pool is.
This still omits the relevant chunks ranked far below 10.
A better reranker still cannot see chunks outside the top 10.
Correct. Retrieve wide, rerank down.

sources.title: BEIR retrieval benchmark — arXiv (Thakur et al.)

questions.scenario: Users ask terse questions such as 'refund window enterprise?', but the corpus contains long policy paragraphs. Dense retrieval on the raw query has low recall.
questions.stem: Which technique specifically embeds an LLM-generated hypothetical answer to retrieve real documents?
options: Reciprocal Rank Fusion.
Matryoshka truncation.
IVFFlat probing.
HyDE (Hypothetical Document Embeddings).
questions.explanation: HyDE has an LLM write a hypothetical answer document for the query, embeds it, and uses that embedding to retrieve real documents. The generated text may contain errors, but it resembles answer passages more than a terse query does. It adds an LLM call per query, so measure the recall gain against the latency cost.
rationales: RRF merges ranked lists; it does not rewrite queries.
Matryoshka truncation shortens embeddings; it does not change the query.
IVFFlat probes control index search breadth, not query content.
Correct. This is exactly the HyDE method.

sources.title: HyDE query rewriting — arXiv (Gao et al.)

questions.scenario: A team wants to apply Contextual Retrieval to 10,000 documents of about 8,000 tokens each, split into 800-token chunks. Generating context means one LLM call per chunk, each including the full document.
questions.stem: What keeps this affordable?
options: Send only the chunk without the document, to save tokens.
Put the full document first in each prompt and use prompt caching, so repeated calls for chunks of the same document reuse the cached prefix.
Generate context only for the first chunk of each document.
Use the largest model available so fewer calls are needed.
questions.explanation: Every chunk of a document shares the same long document prefix, so prompt caching makes the repeated calls cheap. Anthropic estimated about $1.02 per million document tokens, one time, under these same assumptions. Dropping the document would defeat the purpose, because the context must come from the whole document.
rationales: Without the document, the model cannot write document-aware context.
Correct. Cache the shared document prefix across that document's chunk calls.
Later chunks are exactly the ones that lose context.
Model size does not reduce the number of chunks needing context.

questions.scenario: For one query, the labelled set marks 4 chunks as relevant. The top-5 retrieved list contains 2 of them.
questions.stem: What are recall@5 and precision@5?
options: recall@5 = 2, precision@5 = 2
recall@5 = 0.4, precision@5 = 0.5
recall@5 = 0.5, precision@5 = 0.4
recall@5 = 0.5, precision@5 = 0.5
questions.explanation: recall@k is the number of relevant items retrieved in the top k divided by the total number of relevant items: 2/4 = 0.5. precision@k divides the same count by k: 2/5 = 0.4. Contextual Retrieval's headline metric is the related 1 − recall@20.
rationales: Both metrics are fractions, not raw counts.
This swaps the two definitions.
Correct. 2 of 4 relevant found; 2 of 5 retrieved are relevant.
precision@5 divides by k = 5, not by 4.

questions.scenario: You evaluate three queries. The first relevant result is at rank 1 for query 1 and rank 2 for query 2. Query 3 has no relevant result in the retrieved list.
questions.stem: What is the mean reciprocal rank (MRR), counting a query with no relevant result as 0?
questions.explanation: Reciprocal ranks are 1/1 = 1, 1/2 = 0.5 and 0 for the query with no hit. Their mean is 1.5/3 = 0.5. Excluding the failed query would wrongly inflate MRR to 0.75. BEIR describes MRR as a binary, rank-aware metric, which suits a single first-relevant-hit question like this one.
rationales: This would be the result if only query 1 succeeded.
This is the sum of reciprocal ranks, not the mean.
This averages only the two successful queries and hides the failure.

sources.title: BEIR retrieval benchmark — arXiv (Thakur et al.)

questions.scenario: A search team uses graded relevance (0 to 3) and computes nDCG@4 with gain = 2^rel − 1 and discount log2(i + 1) for position i. A query returns documents with relevances [3, 2, 0, 1] in positions 1–4. The ideal ordering is [3, 2, 1, 0].
questions.stem: What is nDCG@4, to three decimal places?
questions.explanation: DCG = 7/1 + 3/log2 3 + 0 + 1/log2 5 ≈ 9.3235, and the ideal DCG = 7 + 3/log2 3 + 1/log2 4 ≈ 9.3928, so nDCG@4 ≈ 0.993. The value 0.985 comes from the linear-gain variant (gain = rel), which is why the gain formula must be stated. The score is below 1 because the relevance-1 document sits below a non-relevant one.
rationales: 0.75 is the share of the top 4 with any relevance, not nDCG.
Correct under the stated 2^rel − 1 gain.
This uses linear gain (rel), not the stated 2^rel − 1.
The order is not ideal (rel 1 sits below rel 0), so the score is below 1.

sources.title: BEIR retrieval benchmark — arXiv (Thakur et al.)
Cumulated gain-based evaluation of IR techniques — ACM TOIS (Järvelin and Kekäläinen)

questions.scenario: A RAG system always passes the top 20 retrieved chunks to the model, which reads all of them. The team wants one retrieval metric that best reflects whether the model had the information it needed.
questions.stem: Which metric fits best?
options: precision@1
MRR
recall@20
nDCG@3
questions.explanation: If the model reads all 20 chunks, what matters most is whether the relevant chunks are among them, which is recall@20. Anthropic's Contextual Retrieval evaluation uses exactly this, reported as the failure rate 1 − recall@20. Position-focused metrics such as MRR and precision@1 suit designs that show one top result.
rationales: precision@1 ignores the other 19 chunks the model sees.
MRR focuses on the first relevant hit, not coverage of all relevant chunks.
Correct. It measures presence of relevant chunks in what the model sees.
nDCG@3 only looks at the top 3 of 20.

questions.scenario: A team is building a labelled set to compare chunking strategies and embedding models for its RAG system before launch.
questions.stem: Which TWO practices make the resulting measurements trustworthy? (Select two.)
options: Sample real user or support queries and have domain experts label the relevant documents or passages, at a level that survives re-chunking.
Tune chunk size and k on a development split and report final numbers on a held-out test split.
Generate all queries with an LLM from the chunks and use them without review.
Judge configurations only by end-to-end answer ratings, without scoring retrieval separately.
questions.explanation: Real queries with expert labels reflect production traffic, and labelling at document or span level keeps the set valid when chunk boundaries change. Tuning on one split and reporting on another avoids optimistic, overfitted numbers. Unreviewed synthetic queries tend to copy chunk wording, and answer-only ratings cannot tell retrieval failures from generation failures.
rationales: Correct. Representative queries and durable labels.
Correct. A held-out split keeps the reported score honest.
Unreviewed synthetic queries mirror the chunk text and flatter lexical matching.
Without a retrieval score you cannot attribute failures to retrieval or generation.

sources.title: BEIR retrieval benchmark — arXiv (Thakur et al.)

questions.scenario: A team plans to replace its BM25 search with a new dense embedding model because the model ranks highly on a public leaderboard. They have not tested it on their own corpus.
questions.stem: What is the best next step?
options: Keep BM25 forever; dense retrieval never outperforms it.
Switch to the dense model and raise top-k to compensate for any loss.
Ship the dense model; leaderboard results transfer to any domain.
Evaluate the dense model against BM25 (and a hybrid of both) on a labelled set from their own corpus before switching.
questions.explanation: The BEIR benchmark found BM25 a robust zero-shot baseline across diverse datasets, and dense models did not uniformly beat it out of domain. Results must be confirmed on your own data, ideally including a hybrid configuration. Raising k hides regressions instead of measuring them.
rationales: Dense and hybrid retrieval often do win; the point is to measure.
Raising k adds cost and does not show whether quality regressed.
Out-of-domain performance varies; leaderboard rank is not proof for your corpus.
Correct. Measure on your own labelled set, with BM25 and hybrid as baselines.

sources.title: BEIR retrieval benchmark — arXiv (Thakur et al.)

questions.scenario: A Claude-based assistant calls a `lookup_order` tool. After running it, the app sends a user message containing the `tool_result` block followed by a text block that says "Here is the data, please continue." The model often replies with a short acknowledgement and stops instead of finishing the task.
questions.stem: What is the most likely fix?
options: Raise max_tokens so the model has room to finish the task.
Send only the tool_result blocks in that user message and move any guidance into the system prompt.
Resend the tool output as a plain text user message instead of a tool_result block.
Remove the tools array from the follow-up request so the model focuses on answering.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's stop-reasons guide says the follow-up message must contain only tool_result blocks, and that adding anything after them ends the assistant turn. The stray text makes the model treat the turn as finished. Guidance belongs in the system prompt, and the same tools array should be kept.
rationales: The model is not running out of tokens; it is ending the turn because of the extra content.
Correct. Only tool_result blocks keep the loop going as intended.
Dropping the structured tool_result breaks the link to the tool_use id and the protocol.
The guide says to keep the same tools array on the follow-up request.

questions.scenario: A travel agent app asks the model to compare flights from three airlines. One response contains three `tool_use` blocks, one per airline API.
questions.stem: How should the app return the results?
options: Run the calls, then send one user message with three tool_result blocks, each with its matching tool_use_id.
Return only the first result and let the model request the others again.
Send three consecutive user messages, each with one tool_result, so each call gets its own turn.
Merge the three outputs into one text block so the model sees a single answer.
questions.explanation: Parallel tool calls are answered together: one user message holding one tool_result per tool_use, matched by id. The independent calls can run concurrently. Splitting or merging the results breaks the mapping the API expects.
rationales: Correct. One message, one result per call, matched by id.
Every tool_use needs a result; dropping two wastes turns and may cause errors.
Results for one assistant turn belong in a single user message.
Merging loses the per-call ids the model uses to match results.
