questions.scenario: A scheduling tool throws an exception when the model passes `date: "next Tuesday"` because it expects ISO 8601. Today the exception bubbles up and the user sees a 500 error.
questions.stem: What is the best way to handle this in the tool loop?
options: Remove the date parameter's type constraint so any string is accepted.
Catch the error and return an empty successful tool_result so the conversation continues.
Retry the same call automatically in a loop until it succeeds.
Catch the error and return a tool_result with is_error set to true and a message such as "date must be ISO 8601, e.g. 2026-03-14".
questions.explanation: Reporting the failure as an error result with an actionable message lets the model correct its input and retry. Anthropic's tool-writing guidance stresses that error messages should tell the agent how to fix the call. Hiding the error or retrying identical input does not fix anything.
rationales: Loosening the schema moves the failure deeper and makes inputs less predictable.
An empty success misleads the model into thinking the meeting was scheduled.
Retrying identical input fails the same way and wastes calls.
Correct. The model reads the error and can resend a valid date.

sources.title: Tool use overview — Claude API docs
Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: An internal research agent occasionally gets stuck calling the same search tool with slight query variations. One run made over 200 calls and cost far more than expected.
questions.stem: Which change most directly prevents this class of failure?
options: Switch to a larger model, which is less likely to loop.
Remove the search tool's description so the model uses it less.
Add stopping conditions to the loop, such as a maximum iteration count and a token or cost budget, and surface the partial result when they trip.
Cache search results so repeated calls are cheaper.
questions.explanation: Building effective agents recommends stopping conditions such as a maximum number of iterations to keep agents under control. A hard cap plus a budget bounds the worst case regardless of model behaviour. The other options may reduce cost per call but do not bound the loop.
rationales: A different model may still loop; it does not guarantee a bound.
A worse description makes tool selection less reliable without stopping loops.
Correct. Explicit limits bound cost and latency for every run.
Caching lowers per-call cost but the loop can still run unbounded.

questions.stem: Which two statements about Claude tool use are accurate? (Select two.)
options: Tool definitions and tool_result blocks are billed as input tokens.
Client tools such as your own functions are executed by Anthropic's servers.
When the model wants a tool, the response has stop_reason "tool_use" and includes tool_use blocks with an id, name and input.
Tool results should be returned in the system prompt of the next request.
questions.explanation: The tool-use overview says tool definitions, tool_use and tool_result blocks are all billed as input, and that a tool request arrives as tool_use blocks with stop_reason tool_use. Client tools run in your application; only server tools run on Anthropic's side. Results go in a user message as tool_result blocks.
rationales: Correct. All of these count toward input tokens.
Client tools run in your app; server tools run on Anthropic's side.
Correct. This is the signal your loop acts on.
Results are sent as tool_result blocks in a user message.

sources.title: Tool use overview — Claude API docs

questions.scenario: A team upgrades an extraction service to a newer Claude model. Their code sets `tool_choice` to force a specific `record_invoice` tool so the output is always JSON. On the new model the request fails with a 400 error.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate change?
options: Retry the request with exponential backoff, since 400 errors are transient.
Use auto tool choice with a clear instruction and a strict schema, or switch to structured outputs since only JSON is needed.
Add a prefilled assistant message starting with "{" to force JSON.
Lower the temperature to zero so the model reliably picks the tool.
questions.explanation: Forced tool choice is not supported on some current Claude models and returns a 400 there. The documented alternatives are auto with strict schemas, or structured outputs when the goal is JSON rather than an action. Prefill and sampling parameters are also unsupported on current models, so they are not fixes.
rationales: A 400 is a request error; retrying the same request fails again.
Correct. This keeps JSON guarantees without forced tool choice.
Prefill is not supported on current Claude models.
Sampling parameters are rejected or ignored on current models and do not force tool use.

sources.title: Tool use overview — Claude API docs

questions.scenario: With OpenAI's Responses API, the model emits a `function_call` item for `get_stock_price`.
questions.stem: How does the app tell the model which call a result belongs to?
options: By sending a function_call_output item with the same call_id.
By repeating the function name in a new user text message.
By putting the result in the instructions field.
Order alone; the first output always matches the first call.
questions.explanation: OpenAI's function-calling guide pairs each function_call with a function_call_output carrying the same call_id. The id, not order or name, links the result to the call. This matters when there are several parallel calls.
rationales: Correct. call_id is the link.
Names are not unique when the same function is called twice.
Instructions are not where tool results go.
Order is not the matching mechanism; ids are.

questions.scenario: A payments agent can call `create_transfer` and then `send_receipt`. In testing, the model sometimes requests both in one response, and the receipt is sent before the transfer exists.
questions.stem: What is the cleanest fix?
options: Sort the tool_use blocks alphabetically before executing them.
Merge both tools into one generic execute_action tool.
Ignore the second tool_use block whenever two arrive.
Disable parallel tool use for this agent so the model requests one tool per turn.
questions.explanation: When tool calls depend on each other, turning off parallel calls makes the model issue them one at a time and see each result first. Claude exposes disable_parallel_tool_use on tool_choice and OpenAI exposes parallel_tool_calls false. Ignoring calls or sorting them only hides the problem.
rationales: Alphabetical order is arbitrary and does not encode dependencies.
A generic tool makes selection and validation harder without fixing ordering.
Every tool_use needs a result; ignoring one breaks the loop.
Correct. Sequential calls respect the dependency.

sources.title: Tool use overview — Claude API docs

questions.scenario: A support inbox receives billing questions, technical bugs and refund requests. Each type needs a different prompt, and refunds need extra policy checks. The categories are stable.
questions.stem: Which pattern fits best?
options: Orchestrator-workers, so a central model invents subtasks per ticket.
Evaluator-optimizer, looping until a grader approves each reply.
Routing: classify the ticket, then send it to a prompt and tools specialised for that category.
A single autonomous agent with every tool and one general prompt.
questions.explanation: Routing is for inputs that fall into distinct categories better handled separately. Classifying first lets each path use its own prompt, tools and checks. The other patterns add cost for a problem whose structure is already known.
rationales: Subtasks are predictable here, so an orchestrator adds needless cost.
Iterative refinement does not address the category split.
Correct. Distinct, stable categories are the routing use case.
One general prompt dilutes per-category instructions and widens tool access.

questions.scenario: A coding assistant must implement feature requests across a large repository. Some requests touch one file; others touch a dozen files in different services, and which files is only clear after reading the code.
questions.stem: Which pattern fits best?
options: Prompt chaining with a fixed sequence of five steps.
Orchestrator-workers: a central model decides which changes are needed and delegates them to workers, then combines the results.
Parallelisation by sectioning, with one worker per top-level folder.
Routing by programming language.
questions.explanation: Orchestrator-workers suits tasks where you can't predict the subtasks needed, and Anthropic names multi-file coding changes as an example. The key difference from parallelisation is that the subtasks are decided at run time. Fixed chains or fixed sections cannot adapt to the request.
rationales: A fixed sequence cannot adapt to how many files a request touches.
Correct. The orchestrator plans subtasks dynamically.
Sectioning splits work fixed in code, not by what the request needs.
Language does not determine which changes a request needs.

questions.scenario: A localisation team translates product copy. Reviewers have a clear rubric (terminology, tone, length limits), and a second pass guided by rubric feedback measurably improves quality.
questions.stem: Which pattern fits best?
options: Evaluator-optimizer: one call drafts, another evaluates against the rubric and gives feedback, and the loop repeats until it passes or hits a limit.
Routing by target language only.
Parallelisation by voting on five translations and picking the most common.
A single call with a longer system prompt.
questions.explanation: Evaluator-optimizer fits when there are clear evaluation criteria and iterative refinement provides measurable value, which is exactly this case. Anthropic names literary translation as an example. A cap on iterations keeps the loop bounded.
rationales: Correct. Clear criteria plus helpful iteration is the defining condition.
Routing may help per language but does not use the rubric feedback.
Voting suits tasks with a single best answer, not refining nuanced text.
A single call ignores the measured gain from iteration.

questions.scenario: A product team wants to generate a weekly report: pull metrics, write a summary, then translate it into three languages. The steps never change. An engineer proposes an autonomous multi-agent framework so the system "can handle anything."
questions.stem: What is the best recommendation?
options: Adopt the multi-agent framework, since agents are more capable than workflows.
Use a single agent with all tools and let it decide the order each week.
Use evaluator-optimizer on every step to maximise quality.
Build a prompt chain with a programmatic check between steps, and add agentic behaviour only if a measured need appears.
questions.explanation: Building effective agents advises finding the simplest solution and adding complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes. The task decomposes cleanly into fixed subtasks, the prompt-chaining case. Agents bring higher cost and compounding errors that buy nothing here.
rationales: Capability is not the constraint; predictability and cost are.
An agent choosing the order of fixed steps adds risk with no benefit.
Iterating on every step adds cost without evidence it is needed.
Correct. Fixed steps map to a chain with gates.

questions.scenario: A team needs high confidence when flagging code for security vulnerabilities. They run the same review prompt several times and flag the code if enough runs find an issue.
questions.stem: Which pattern is this?
options: Prompt chaining.
Orchestrator-workers.
Parallelisation by voting.
Routing.
questions.explanation: Parallelisation has two variants: sectioning, which splits a task into independent parts, and voting, which runs the same task several times to get diverse outputs or consensus. Anthropic uses reviewing code for vulnerabilities as a voting example. Thresholds on the votes trade false positives against false negatives.
rationales: Chaining runs different steps in sequence, not the same step repeatedly.
There is no central model deciding subtasks.
Correct. Several runs of one task combined by vote.
Nothing is being classified into categories.

questions.scenario: An agent has 35 tools, including `search_docs`, `find_documents`, `docs_lookup` and `query_kb`, which all search the same knowledge base with slightly different filters. Logs show it picks among them almost at random.
questions.stem: What is the best first change?
options: Add a system-prompt line saying "choose the best tool carefully."
Consolidate the overlapping tools into one well-described search tool with filter parameters, and namespace tools by service.
Add more tools so each filter combination has its own dedicated tool.
Shorten every description to one line so the tool list uses fewer tokens.
questions.explanation: Anthropic recommends fewer, targeted tools and namespacing, and notes that if a human can't say which tool to use, an agent can't either. One search tool with explicit filters removes the ambiguity. Generic exhortations or shorter descriptions make selection worse, not better.
rationales: A vague instruction does not remove the overlap that causes confusion.
Correct. Fewer, distinct, clearly described tools are easier to choose between.
More overlapping tools increase the confusion.
Detailed descriptions are what help the model choose correctly.

sources.title: Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: A `list_customers` tool returns the raw CRM payload: thousands of records, each with dozens of internal fields and UUIDs. The agent's context fills after two calls and answers degrade.
questions.stem: Which redesign best follows tool-writing guidance?
options: Return high-signal fields such as names and readable ids, paginate with a sensible default page size, note when results are truncated, and offer a concise or detailed format.
Return only the first record so the output is always small.
Keep the payload but switch to a model with a larger context window.
Compress the JSON by removing whitespace.
questions.explanation: Writing tools for agents recommends returning meaningful, high-signal fields, a response_format option, and pagination and truncation with sensible defaults. Telling the model output was truncated lets it ask for more. A bigger window postpones the problem and wastes tokens on noise.
rationales: Correct. This keeps outputs small and useful.
One record makes the tool useless for most tasks.
A larger window still fills with low-value tokens and costs more.
Whitespace is a small part of the problem; the volume of low-signal data remains.

sources.title: Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: A file-editing tool accepts paths relative to the current directory. After the agent changes directories, its edits frequently land in the wrong files.
questions.stem: Following Anthropic's agent-computer interface advice, what is the best fix?
options: Ask the user to confirm each edit.
Add a warning to the system prompt about relative paths.
Let the tool guess the intended directory from the file name.
Change the tool to require absolute file paths.
questions.explanation: Building effective agents describes exactly this: the model erred with relative paths, so the team changed the tool to always require absolute file paths, after which the model used it flawlessly. Designing the input so the mistake is impossible (poka-yoke) beats instructing the model to avoid it. Confirmation adds friction without removing the cause.
rationales: Confirmation slows work and still lets wrong paths through.
Instructions are weaker than an interface that prevents the mistake.
Guessing adds a new source of silent errors.
Correct. Changing the interface removes the error class.

questions.scenario: A customer-service agent has an `issue_refund(order_id, amount)` tool. After a network timeout, the agent retries the call and the customer is refunded twice. The team already requires human approval for refunds over a threshold.
questions.stem: What change most directly prevents duplicate refunds?
options: Lower the approval threshold so a human approves every refund.
Tell the model in the system prompt never to retry refund calls.
Make the tool idempotent: require an idempotency key per refund intent and have the backend ignore repeats of the same key.
Increase the tool's timeout so it never times out.
questions.explanation: Agents and their harnesses retry, and the OpenAI Agents SDK docs note that approval permits a tool call to execute but does not guarantee exactly-once execution; they recommend a stable idempotency key per logical action. An idempotency key makes a repeated call safe by design. Prompt instructions and longer timeouts reduce the odds but do not remove the duplicate path.
rationales: Approval controls whether to act, not whether a retried call runs twice.
Retries can also come from the harness, and prompts are not guarantees.
Correct. The backend deduplicates repeated requests.
Timeouts can still happen; the retry path still double-charges.

sources.title: Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 — OWASP GenAI

questions.scenario: An analytics agent answers questions over a production database. It currently connects with the application's admin credentials and has `run_sql`, `drop_table` and `update_rows` tools available.
questions.stem: Which two changes best apply least privilege? (Select two.)
options: Give the agent a read-only, scoped database role and remove the write and drop tools it does not need.
Keep admin credentials so queries never fail on permissions.
Require human approval for any remaining high-impact action, enforced outside the model.
Add "never modify data" to the system prompt as the main safeguard.
questions.explanation: OWASP LLM06 Excessive Agency covers excessive functionality, permissions and autonomy, and the fixes are to cut each one. Scoped read-only credentials and removing unneeded tools limit what can go wrong. Approval enforced in code limits autonomy; a prompt instruction is not an access control.
rationales: Correct. Reduces both functionality and permissions.
Admin credentials are the excessive permission the item warns about.
Correct. Reduces autonomy for actions that remain.
Prompt instructions can be ignored or overridden, for example by injection.

sources.title: Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 — OWASP GenAI

questions.scenario: A tool is defined as `get(user, q)` with the description "Gets data." The model often passes an email address in `user` when the backend expects a numeric id.
questions.stem: What is the best improvement?
options: Keep the name and add an example in the user's message each time.
Rename the parameter to user_id, describe its format, and write a detailed description of what the tool returns and when to use it.
Accept any value and try both lookups in the backend.
Shorten the description further so it costs fewer tokens.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance asks for unambiguous parameter names such as user_id and extremely detailed tool descriptions. The name and description are the model's only documentation of the tool. Better names fix the root cause instead of compensating elsewhere.
rationales: Repeating examples in every message is fragile and wastes tokens.
Correct. Clear names and descriptions prevent the wrong input.
Guessing in the backend hides errors and can return the wrong user.
A shorter description removes the information the model needs.

sources.title: Writing tools for agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: A developer's IDE connects to three MCP servers: one for Git, one for a ticket tracker and one for a database.
questions.stem: How many MCP clients are involved, and what is the IDE's role?
options: Three clients, one per server; the IDE is the host.
One client shared by all three servers; the IDE is a server.
Three hosts, one per server; the IDE is the client.
No clients; the IDE talks to servers directly as a peer.
questions.explanation: MCP defines hosts (the LLM application), clients (connectors within the host) and servers. Each client keeps a connection to one server. So one IDE host runs three clients for three servers.
rationales: Correct. One host, one client per server.
Clients are one per server, and the IDE is the host.
There is one host here: the IDE.
Clients are the connectors the host uses to talk to servers.

questions.scenario: A team is building an MCP server for its documentation platform. It wants (a) page content the app can attach as context, (b) a "summarise this page" template the user picks from a menu, and (c) a `create_page` action the model can call.
questions.stem: Which mapping of MCP primitives is correct?
options: (a) tool, (b) resource, (c) prompt
(a) prompt, (b) tool, (c) resource
(a) resource, (b) tool, (c) tool
(a) resource, (b) prompt, (c) tool
questions.explanation: The MCP spec defines resources as context and data, prompts as templated messages and workflows for users, and tools as functions for the AI model to execute. Page content is a resource, the user-chosen template is a prompt and the action the model calls is a tool. Choosing the right primitive also decides who controls it.
rationales: This swaps all three roles.
Prompts are user templates, not data, and resources are not actions.
A user-selected template is a prompt, not a tool.
Correct. Data, user template, model-invoked function.

questions.scenario: A local MCP server launched by a desktop host over stdio works in unit tests, but in the host it fails with JSON parse errors. The developer recently added `print()` statements for debugging.
questions.stem: What is the most likely cause and fix?
options: The host needs a session id; add an Mcp-Session-Id header.
stdio servers must use OAuth; configure an access token.
Debug output on stdout is corrupting the newline-delimited JSON-RPC stream; write logs to stderr.
The server must switch to Streamable HTTP for any debugging.
questions.explanation: With the stdio transport, the server reads newline-delimited JSON-RPC from stdin and writes it to stdout. The spec says the server must not write anything to stdout that is not a valid MCP message, and may write logs to stderr. Debug prints on stdout break the client's parsing.
rationales: The session header is an HTTP concept and is removed in 2026-07-28.
Authorization is for HTTP; stdio servers get credentials from the environment.
Correct. stdout is the protocol channel.
stdio supports debugging fine once logs go to stderr.

questions.scenario: A remote MCP server wraps a company's internal REST API. To keep things simple, the developer plans to accept whatever bearer token the client sends and forward it unchanged to the internal API.
questions.stem: What does the MCP authorization spec require instead?
options: Forwarding is fine as long as the connection uses TLS.
The server must validate that tokens were issued for it (audience) and must not accept or pass through tokens meant for other services; it obtains its own credentials for upstream calls.
The client should put the upstream token in the URL query string so the server can read it easily.
The server should skip validation because the host already authenticated the user.
questions.explanation: In MCP, a remote server is an OAuth 2.1 resource server and must validate the token audience. The spec says MCP servers must not accept or transit any other tokens, which rules out token passthrough. Tokens belong in the Authorization header, never in the query string.
rationales: TLS protects transport but does not fix accepting tokens meant for others.
Correct. Audience validation and no passthrough.
Tokens must not appear in the URI query string.
The server must validate tokens itself.

questions.stem: A team is updating an MCP client to the 2026-07-28 specification. Which two changes reflect that revision? (Select two.)
options: The initialize handshake is removed; each request carries the protocol version and client capabilities in _meta.
Sampling becomes a required client feature.
Protocol sessions and the Mcp-Session-Id header are removed; cross-call state uses explicit server-minted handles.
Servers must keep a long-lived session per client to track state.
questions.explanation: The 2026-07-28 changelog makes MCP stateless: initialize is gone, and the protocol version and client capabilities travel in each request's _meta. Sessions and the Mcp-Session-Id header are removed in favour of explicit handles. Sampling is deprecated, not required.
rationales: Correct. Per-request metadata replaces the handshake.
Sampling is deprecated in this revision.
Correct. State moves to explicit handles.
This contradicts the stateless design.

questions.scenario: A mobile client connects to a remote MCP server and, to avoid header handling, appends `?access_token=...` to the MCP endpoint URL.
questions.stem: What should it do instead?
options: Send the token in the Authorization: Bearer header on every request.
Keep the query parameter but shorten the token lifetime.
Put the token inside the JSON-RPC params of each tool call.
Drop authorization because remote servers do not need it.
questions.explanation: The MCP authorization spec says access tokens go in the Authorization Bearer header and must not be included in the URI query string. URLs leak into logs, history and proxies. Putting tokens in tool arguments exposes them to the model's context.
rationales: Correct. This is the required placement.
Shorter lifetimes do not make query-string tokens compliant.
Tool parameters end up in model context and logs.
A server exposing protected data should require authorization.

questions.scenario: A chat host lets users install third-party MCP servers. One server marks its `delete_files` tool with an annotation saying it is read-only, and the host is considering auto-running tools that carry that hint.
questions.stem: Which two practices align with MCP's security principles? (Select two.)
options: Treat tool annotations from untrusted servers as untrusted hints, not as guarantees.
Auto-approve any tool annotated as read-only to reduce prompts.
Obtain explicit user consent before invoking tools, with clear information about what the tool will do.
Rely on the server to ask for consent, since the host only displays results.
questions.explanation: The MCP spec states that tools represent arbitrary code execution and that annotations should be considered untrusted unless they come from a trusted server. It also places consent on the host: hosts must obtain explicit user consent before invoking any tool. A malicious server can label anything as read-only.
rationales: Correct. Annotations are only as trustworthy as the server.
This lets a malicious server bypass consent with a label.
Correct. Consent is the host's responsibility.
The spec assigns consent to the host, not the server.

questions.scenario: A coding agent runs for hours. Its context is mostly old test outputs and file listings from early steps, and quality drops as the window fills.
questions.stem: Which change is the safest first step?
options: Paste the full repository into the system prompt so the agent never needs tools.
Start each step in a fresh context with no history.
Raise the max output token limit.
Clear old raw tool results the agent no longer needs, keeping recent ones and the conversation's decisions.
questions.explanation: Effective context engineering describes tool-result clearing as one of the safest forms of compaction. Old raw outputs are rarely needed once the agent has acted on them. Wiping all history loses decisions, and loading everything makes the window problem worse.
rationales: This floods the context and contradicts just-in-time retrieval.
Losing all history drops decisions and progress.
Output length is not the problem; input context is.
Correct. Low risk, high savings.

questions.scenario: A research assistant must survey dozens of sources on a topic. A single agent's context overflows with search results long before it can write the synthesis.
questions.stem: Which architecture best addresses this?
options: Give the single agent a larger output token limit.
Have every sub-agent return its full raw search results to the lead.
A lead agent that delegates focused searches to sub-agents, each working in its own context and returning a condensed summary.
Run the same agent several times and keep the longest answer.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's context-engineering and multi-agent posts describe sub-agents that explore in clean context windows and return condensed summaries, often 1,000 to 2,000 tokens. The lead keeps a clean context for synthesis. Returning raw results would recreate the overflow in the lead.
rationales: The bottleneck is input context, not output length.
Raw results defeat the purpose of sub-agents.
Correct. Isolation plus condensed summaries.
Repetition does not fix the context overflow.

questions.scenario: A personal assistant agent should remember a user's preferences across weeks of separate sessions. An engineer proposes relying on the provider's automatic compaction to keep that history.
questions.stem: What is the best response?
options: Agree; compaction preserves everything important indefinitely.
Compaction manages a single context window; persist durable facts in a memory store or notes and inject the relevant ones per session.
Store the full transcript of every session in the system prompt.
Fine-tune the model weekly on the user's conversations.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's agent-memory research describes compaction as a context-window tool, not long-term memory. Durable facts belong in memory notes or representations that are retrieved and injected as needed. Stuffing all transcripts into the prompt does not scale.
rationales: Compaction summarises within a window and can drop details; it is not a memory system.
Correct. Separate memory layer, selective injection.
Full transcripts grow without bound and dilute attention.
Fine-tuning is costly and slow for per-user preferences.

sources.title: Components of agent memory — Anthropic Research

questions.scenario: An agent saves notes after each session. Weeks later it confidently states a customer's contract renewal date that is wrong. Investigation shows an earlier note recorded the date incorrectly, and later sessions trusted it.
questions.stem: Which practice most directly addresses this?
options: Verify memory notes against the source transcripts, for example during consolidation, before they are trusted.
Delete all memory after each session.
Only record failures in memory so notes stay short.
Increase the number of notes saved per session.
questions.explanation: Anthropic's agent-memory research warns that a note that is wrong from the start, or drifts as things change, can still be trusted in a later session. Its consolidation pass tests notes against the original transcripts. The same research found that a record-only-failures rule reduced the benefit of memory.
rationales: Correct. Checking notes against sources catches errors.
Deleting memory removes its value entirely.
The research found this rule reduced memory gains.
More notes do not make wrong notes correct.

sources.title: Components of agent memory — Anthropic Research

questions.scenario: A codebase Q&A agent loads every file in a 2,000-file repository into its prompt at the start of each task. Costs are high and answers miss details buried in the middle.
questions.stem: Which approach does context-engineering guidance recommend?
options: Keep loading all files but put the most important ones at the end.
Split the repository into four prompts and send them in parallel.
Summarise the whole repository once and never let the agent read source files.
Keep lightweight references such as file paths in context and give the agent tools to search and read files just in time.
questions.explanation: Effective context engineering recommends just-in-time retrieval: keep lightweight identifiers in context and load data through tools when needed. This keeps the window small and focused. Loading everything up front wastes tokens and dilutes attention.
rationales: Reordering does not fix the cost or dilution of loading everything.
Parallel prompts each lack the full picture and cannot cross-reference.
A fixed summary loses the details questions need.
Correct. Progressive, on-demand loading.

questions.scenario: A team designs a memory layer for an agent that tracks many vendor contracts, each with about a dozen facts. Option A stores all facts in one shared table; option B keeps one page per vendor. They also debate whether to record only failed interactions.
questions.stem: Which two design choices are supported by Anthropic's agent-memory research? (Select two.)
options: Organise memory as one page per entity rather than a single shared table.
Record only failures to keep memory small.
Record what worked as well as what failed.
Rely on compaction summaries as the memory store.
questions.explanation: In Anthropic's memory research, one shared table kept 41 of 57 contract facts while one page per entity kept all 57. A record-only-failures rule cut the memory gain. Compaction is described as a context-window tool, not long-term memory.
rationales: Correct. Per-entity pages preserved every fact in the study.
The study found this rule reduced the benefit of memory.
Correct. Avoids the loss seen with failures-only notes.
Compaction is not a long-term memory mechanism.

sources.title: Components of agent memory — Anthropic Research

questions.scenario: A support assistant's system prompt was edited to fix a formatting complaint. A week later, users report that it has stopped asking for order numbers before issuing refunds. Nobody noticed during the change because the engineer tested the formatting case by hand.
questions.stem: Which practice would most directly have caught this before release?
options: Lowering the temperature so the assistant behaves more consistently after edits
Reading the provider's release notes before each deployment
Having the engineer manually try five extra prompts after each edit
A regression eval set built from real conversations, run automatically on every prompt or model change
questions.explanation: Prompt edits can fix one case and break others, so a regression suite drawn from real traffic and run on every change is the safety net. OpenAI's guidance is to treat prompts as application code and run evaluation checks with every deployment. Manual spot checks only cover the cases the engineer thinks of.
rationales: Temperature does not detect regressions, and many current models reject or ignore sampling parameters anyway.
Release notes cover provider changes, but this regression came from the team's own prompt edit.
A handful of manual checks covers only what the engineer remembers to try; the refund behaviour was exactly what was missed.
Correct. A regression suite from real traffic, run on every change, covers behaviours the editor was not looking at.

sources.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: A team is about to launch an internal coding agent and has no evals. The lead proposes waiting until they can generate 2,000 synthetic tasks so the results are statistically meaningful.
questions.stem: What is the better way to start?
options: Use a public coding benchmark only, since it is already large and well known
Begin with 20 to 50 unambiguous tasks drawn from real failures and usage, and grow the set over time
Skip offline evals and rely on user thumbs-down after launch
Generate the 2,000 synthetic tasks first, because small sets are useless
questions.explanation: Anthropic's agent-evals guidance is to start with 20 to 50 tasks drawn from real failures, where two experts would agree on pass or fail. A small, realistic set catches real regressions now and grows as new failures appear. Waiting for a huge synthetic set delays any signal.
rationales: Public benchmarks rarely reflect your own tasks, tools and failure modes.
Correct. A small set of real, unambiguous tasks gives useful signal immediately and grows from production failures.
Online feedback is valuable but arrives after users are affected, and it is not a pre-release gate.
Small sets have wide error bars but still catch regressions; delaying all evaluation is worse.

sources.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: A capability suite of multi-step data-analysis tasks started at 18% pass rate. After six months of prompt and tool work it has passed above 98% for four consecutive releases.
questions.stem: What should the team do with this suite?
options: Move it into the regression suite and write new, harder capability tasks
Delete it, since it no longer tells the team anything
Keep reporting it as the headline capability metric
Raise the pass threshold to 100% and keep it as a capability eval
questions.explanation: Capability evals start low; once a suite saturates it graduates into the regression suite, where a near-100% rate is expected and any drop is a real signal. New capability tasks are then needed to keep measuring progress.
rationales: Correct. Saturated capability tasks become regression tasks, and harder capability tasks replace them.
The tasks still protect against regressions; deleting them throws away a safety net.
A saturated suite cannot show further capability gains, so it is a poor headline capability metric.
Changing the threshold does not make a saturated suite measure new capability.

sources.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: A travel agent eval checks that the agent calls search_flights, then hold_seat, then confirm_booking, in that order. A new model finds the same flight via a cached itinerary tool and books it correctly, but the eval marks it as a failure. Another engineer proposes switching to an LLM judge that reads the agent's final message and checks whether it says the booking succeeded.
questions.stem: What is the best way to grade this task?
options: Use the LLM judge on the agent's final message, since it accepts any path
Keep the tool-order check and add an instruction forcing the agent to use search_flights first
Check the final environment state: a booking exists with the correct passenger, dates and fare
Grade by comparing the full transcript with a reference transcript
questions.explanation: Agent evals should grade the outcome, meaning the real end state, not the path taken. Checking a fixed tool order fails valid solutions, and grading the agent's own claim trusts exactly what you are trying to verify.
rationales: The agent's message is a claim, not the outcome; it can say the booking succeeded when it did not.
Forcing a path overfits the prompt to the grader and still rejects other valid solutions.
Correct. Verifying the booking in the environment accepts any valid path and rejects false claims.
Matching a reference transcript is even stricter than checking tool order and fails valid alternative paths.

sources.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: An invoice-extraction feature returns JSON with vendor_name, invoice_date, currency and total. The team has 300 labelled invoices with the correct values.
questions.stem: Which grading approach fits best?
options: Pairwise comparison between the new and old prompt's outputs
Code: validate the JSON against the schema and compare each field with the label, with normalisation for dates and amounts
Human review of every output on each pull request
An LLM judge with a 1 to 10 rubric for extraction quality
questions.explanation: When correctness is a checkable property, code-based graders are fast, cheap and reproducible. Schema validation plus field comparison against labels decides pass or fail exactly, so a model judge adds cost and noise without adding information.
rationales: Pairwise preference does not tell you whether the extracted values are right.
Correct. Labelled fields and a known schema are ideal for deterministic code checks.
Human review of every output is slow and expensive, and adds nothing over checking against labels.
A model judge is non-deterministic and needs calibration, which is unnecessary when exact labels exist.

sources.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: A team needs to evaluate customer-support replies for accuracy against the help-centre article, empathy and whether they resolve the question. There is no single correct reply.
questions.stem: Which grading setup is most appropriate?
options: A regex check that the reply contains the customer's name and a greeting
No grading; open-ended replies cannot be evaluated
Exact-match comparison with one reference reply written by a support agent
An LLM judge with a per-criterion rubric and the relevant article as reference, calibrated against expert human labels on a sample
questions.explanation: Open-ended output with several acceptable answers calls for a model-based grader with a clear rubric and reference material. Because model graders are non-deterministic and biased, they must be calibrated against human labels before they are trusted.
rationales: A regex checks surface features, not accuracy or resolution.
Open-ended quality can be graded with rubrics, model judges and human review.
Exact match against one reference rejects every other good reply.
Correct. A rubric judge handles open-ended quality, and human calibration checks it measures what you care about.

Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena — arXiv

questions.scenario: A pairwise LLM judge compares the production prompt (always shown as Response A) with a candidate (always Response B). The candidate wins 61% of comparisons. A reviewer reruns a sample with the order reversed and the production prompt now wins most of them.
questions.stem: What is the most appropriate change to the evaluation?
options: Raise the judge's temperature so position effects average out
Add "be fair and ignore the order" to the judge prompt and keep the single ordering
Always put the candidate first so it is judged more strictly
Run each comparison in both orders, aggregate the verdicts, and count order-inconsistent pairs as ties
questions.explanation: This is position bias, which Wang et al. showed can flip pairwise outcomes simply by changing the order. Their Balanced Position Calibration evaluates both orders and aggregates, so a verdict that depends on order does not count as a win.
rationales: Temperature does not correct position bias and is unsupported or ignored on many current models.
An instruction does not remove a systematic bias; the order must be controlled in the procedure.
Any fixed order bakes in the bias; it only changes which side benefits.
Correct. Swapping positions and aggregating removes the order effect; inconsistent pairs are treated as ties.

sources.title: Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators — arXiv

questions.scenario: A new prompt makes answers about 70% longer. A pairwise judge from a different model family, run in both orders, prefers the new prompt 68% of the time. A blind human review of 50 pairs shows no clear preference, and several reviewers say the longer answers pad the content.
questions.stem: What is the most likely explanation for the gap?
options: Verbosity bias: the judge favours longer answers that are not actually better
Position bias: the judge favours whichever answer comes first
Self-preference bias: the judge favours its own generations
The human sample is too small, so the judge's result should be trusted
questions.explanation: Zheng et al. documented verbosity bias, where LLM judges prefer longer responses. Position bias is ruled out because both orders were run, and self-preference is unlikely with a judge from a different family. The human disagreement is exactly the calibration signal to act on.
rationales: Correct. A large length change, a judge win and no human preference point to verbosity bias.
Running both orders controls for position bias.
The judge is from a different model family, so self-preference is not the likely cause.
Disagreement with human labels is a reason to distrust the judge, not to dismiss the humans.

sources.title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena — arXiv

questions.scenario: A team is choosing between a model from Vendor X and one from Vendor Y for a writing assistant. To save time they plan to use Vendor X's model as the pairwise judge.
questions.stem: What is the main risk, and how should they address it?
options: Position bias only, which they can fix by always listing Vendor Y first
Verbosity bias only, which they can fix by truncating both outputs to the same length
Self-preference: the judge may favour its own family's outputs, so use a judge from a different family or a panel and check against human labels
No risk, because strong judges agree with humans over 80% of the time
questions.explanation: LLM evaluators recognise and favour their own generations, and self-recognition correlates with the strength of self-preference. When the judge's own family is one of the contestants, use an independent judge or a panel and validate against human labels.
rationales: Position bias is real but is fixed by swapping orders, not by a fixed order, and it is not the main risk in this setup.
Truncation damages outputs and does not address the judge favouring its own family.
Correct. Self-preference is the specific risk here; an independent judge plus human calibration addresses it.
High average agreement does not remove systematic self-preference in a comparison that includes the judge's own model.

sources.title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations — arXiv

questions.scenario: An LLM judge will gate releases of a medical-information summariser. The team wants evidence the judge can be trusted.
questions.stem: Which validation step gives the most meaningful evidence?
options: Ask the judge to report a confidence score and keep only high-confidence verdicts
Use the most capable model available as the judge, which makes validation unnecessary
Run the judge three times on the same outputs and confirm it gives the same scores
Have clinicians label a sample with the same rubric and compare judge-human agreement with clinician-clinician agreement
questions.explanation: Model-based graders need calibration against human labels. Comparing judge-human agreement with human-human agreement shows whether the judge matches expert judgment, as the MT-Bench study did. Consistency across runs shows only that it is stable, not that it is right.
rationales: Self-reported confidence is itself unvalidated and does not show agreement with experts.
Even strong judges show position, verbosity and self-preference biases, so they still need calibration.
Self-consistency is not correctness; a judge can be consistently wrong.
Correct. Agreement with expert labels, benchmarked against inter-expert agreement, is the calibration evidence that matters.

questions.stem: Which two biases are documented in the primary research on LLM-as-judge evaluation? (Select two.)
options: Position bias: verdicts change when the order of the answers is swapped
Verbosity bias: judges tend to favour longer answers
Brevity bias: judges consistently prefer the shortest answer
Order immunity: a detailed rubric removes any effect of answer order
questions.explanation: Zheng et al. describe position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, and Wang et al. show that order alone can flip outcomes. The documented length effect runs toward longer answers, and no study shows a rubric alone makes judges immune to order.
rationales: Correct. Wang et al. showed outcomes flip with the order of appearance.
Correct. Zheng et al. found judges favour longer, more verbose responses.
The documented effect is the opposite: a preference for longer answers.
Position bias has to be controlled procedurally, for example by swapping orders; a rubric does not remove it.

questions.scenario: A classifier prompt scores 0.82 accuracy on a 400-question eval set with pass/fail grading.
questions.stem: Which is the approximate 95% confidence interval for the accuracy?
questions.explanation: For binary scores, SE = sqrt(p(1 − p)/n) = sqrt(0.82 × 0.18 / 400) ≈ 0.0192. The 95% interval is mean ± 1.96 × SE ≈ ±0.038, so about [0.782, 0.858].
rationales: This uses one SE as the half-width, which is roughly a 68% interval, not 95%.
This badly understates the uncertainty, as if the sample were many times larger.
This doubles the correct half-width.

sources.title: Adding Error Bars to Evals — arXiv

questions.scenario: Prompts A and B are each run on the same 500 questions. A scores 0.78 and B scores 0.81. An engineer computes a 95% CI for each, sees that they overlap, and concludes there is no evidence B is better.
questions.stem: What is the better analysis?
options: Rerun only prompt B on a fresh set of 500 questions and compare with A's original score
Pick B anyway, because a higher mean is always the better choice
Compute per-question score differences and the paired standard error, which accounts for the positive correlation between A and B on the same questions
Accept the conclusion, because overlapping confidence intervals mean no significant difference
questions.explanation: When two systems answer the same questions, their scores are correlated, and the paired standard error SE(A − B) = sqrt(SE_A² + SE_B² − 2·SE_A·SE_B·Corr) is smaller than the independent one. Overlapping individual intervals are not a valid test of the difference.
rationales: Using different questions for each prompt throws away the pairing and adds variance.
A higher mean on a sample can be noise; the difference needs an error bar.
Correct. Paired differences use the shared questions and usually give a much tighter estimate.
Overlapping separate intervals can hide a real difference that a paired test detects.

sources.title: Adding Error Bars to Evals — arXiv

questions.scenario: A reading-comprehension eval has 600 questions built from 60 passages, 10 questions per passage. The team reports accuracy with the standard error computed as if all 600 questions were independent.
questions.stem: What is the problem, and what should they report instead?
options: They should drop to one question per passage, since multiple questions per passage are invalid
Nothing is wrong; more questions always means independent evidence
The naive SE understates uncertainty because questions within a passage are correlated; report a clustered SE by passage and the number of clusters
They should report the median instead of the mean to remove the clustering
questions.explanation: Questions that share a passage are not independent, so the naive SE is too small. Miller recommends clustered standard errors for grouped questions, which can be about three times the naive value, and reporting the number of clusters.
rationales: Grouped questions are fine as long as the analysis accounts for the clustering.
Correlated questions add less information than independent ones, so the naive SE is overconfident.
Correct. Cluster by passage and report the cluster count; that is what actually limits precision.
Changing the statistic does not fix the dependence between questions.

sources.title: Adding Error Bars to Evals — arXiv

questions.scenario: The same prompt and model, run on the same eval set on different days, score 71%, 79% and 74%. The team wants a stable number for release decisions.
questions.stem: What should they do?
options: Remove any task whose result changes between runs
Run several trials per question, report the mean with its standard error, and log infrastructure errors separately from task failures
Set temperature to 0 so every run gives the same answer
Report the best of the three runs
questions.explanation: Run-to-run variation is real sampling noise, and resampling K answers per question reduces it. Miller advises against lowering the temperature to cut variance because it changes the system being measured, and current models often reject or ignore sampling parameters.
rationales: Silently dropping unstable tasks hides ambiguity and real weaknesses; read their transcripts instead.
Correct. Repeated trials with an error bar, plus separating infrastructure noise, gives an honest, stable estimate.
This changes the system you are measuring and is unsupported or ignored on many current models.
Cherry-picking the best run is biased upward.

sources.title: Adding Error Bars to Evals — arXiv

questions.scenario: A customer-facing billing agent succeeds on a given task 75% of the time per independent trial. Product requires that it handle the task correctly for each of three different customers who ask it.
questions.stem: Which metric matches the requirement, and what is its value?
questions.explanation: When every attempt must succeed, the relevant metric is pass^k, the probability that all k trials succeed: 0.75³ ≈ 0.42. pass@k measures at least one success in k, which suits retry-and-select settings, not a customer-facing agent.
rationales: pass@3 is the chance at least one of three succeeds, which overstates reliability for this requirement.
This is the chance that at least one of the three fails, not the success metric asked for.
Correct. All three must succeed: 0.75³ = 0.421875.
This is the per-trial rate, not the chance that all three customers are served correctly.

sources.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: In a new agent eval, one task scores 0 out of 30 trials across three different models, while the models do well on similar tasks.
questions.stem: What should the team do first?
options: Conclude that current models cannot do this task and remove it from the roadmap
Increase the number of trials to 300 to get a more precise estimate
Read the transcripts and check the task and grader for errors
Switch to a stronger LLM judge for this task
questions.explanation: A 0% pass rate over many trials usually indicates a broken task, such as an impossible requirement, a wrong expected answer or a grader that cannot parse valid output. Anthropic stresses reading transcripts, and reports large score jumps once grading bugs were fixed.
rationales: Concluding incapability without inspecting the task risks acting on a grading bug.
More trials of a broken task only make the wrong number more precise.
Correct. Transcripts reveal whether the task or the grader is broken before anyone draws conclusions.
Changing graders without diagnosing the failure may hide the bug rather than fix it.

sources.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: A team's 200-question eval for a new prompt shows accuracy rising from 80% to 83% (independent runs, pass/fail scoring). The product manager wants to announce a 3-point improvement.
questions.stem: What is the most defensible conclusion?
options: The change is within noise: SE per arm is about 2.8 points, and detecting 3 points reliably needs thousands of questions, or a paired analysis on the same questions
The eval is broken because 200 questions cannot produce a confidence interval
The improvement is real because 3 points is more than one standard error
The improvement is real because the new score is higher
questions.explanation: At 80% on 200 questions, SE = sqrt(0.16/200) ≈ 0.028, so each 95% half-width is about 5.5 points, and the independent difference has an SE of about 3.9 points. A power calculation for a 3-point difference near 80% gives roughly 2,800 questions per arm, which pairing reduces.
rationales: Correct. The difference is smaller than its error bar; more questions or a paired design are needed.
A small set still gives a valid, if wide, confidence interval.
The SE of the difference is about 3.9 points, so 3 points is less than one SE of the difference, far from significant.
A higher sample mean can easily arise from noise at this sample size.

sources.title: Adding Error Bars to Evals — arXiv

questions.scenario: A team is adding evals to CI for a repository that contains prompts, tool definitions and the pinned model ID.
questions.stem: Which setup is the most practical?
options: Run one example prompt per pull request to confirm the model still responds
On every pull request that touches prompts, tools or the model ID, run fast code checks and the regression suite; run the larger model-graded suites on merge or nightly
Run human review of a sample of outputs on every pull request instead of automated checks
Run evals only once a quarter against production, to avoid slowing CI
questions.explanation: Treat prompts as application code and run evaluation checks with every change, as OpenAI's prompting guide recommends. Layering cheap deterministic checks and the regression suite on each pull request with heavier model-graded suites less often balances speed and coverage.
rationales: One example is a smoke test, not regression safety.
Correct. Fast checks gate every change, and the more expensive suites still run regularly.
Human review is too slow for every pull request; it belongs in calibration and audits.
Quarterly evals let regressions ship for months.

sources.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: A new prompt for a support bot passes the offline regression suite and improves the model-graded quality score. The team plans the production rollout.
questions.stem: What is the best rollout plan?
options: Ship to 100% of traffic, since it already passed offline evals
Canary the prompt to a small share of traffic against a concurrent control, with a primary metric, guardrail metrics and rollback thresholds agreed in advance
Ship to a small share of traffic and watch only the resolution rate
Ship to 100% and compare this week's resolution rate with last week's
questions.explanation: Offline evals only cover the cases you anticipated, so changes should be exposed gradually and compared with a control group served at the same time, as the SRE Workbook describes for canarying. Guardrails and rollback thresholds set in advance stop a change that helps one metric while hurting latency, cost or safety.
rationales: Offline success does not guarantee real-traffic behaviour, and a full rollout exposes every user to any regression.
Correct. A concurrent control, predefined guardrails and rollback rules make the rollout both measurable and safe.
Watching only the primary metric misses regressions in latency, cost, refusals or safety.
A before/after comparison is confounded by traffic mix, seasonality and other changes.

questions.scenario: A support bot's A/B test has resolution rate as its primary metric.
questions.stem: Which two are appropriate guardrail metrics to monitor alongside it? (Select two.)
options: Last month's offline judge win rate on the golden set
Number of lines changed in the prompt file
Cost per resolved conversation
p95 response latency
questions.explanation: Guardrail metrics are live measures the change is not meant to improve but must not worsen. Latency is one of Google SRE's golden signals, and cost per resolved conversation catches a change that wins on resolution by spending far more tokens.
rationales: An offline score from last month does not measure the live variants in the test.
Prompt diff size says nothing about user-facing behaviour.
Correct. Cost per outcome catches regressions in token spend that the primary metric hides.
Correct. Latency is a core operational signal that a prompt change can degrade.

sources.title: Monitoring distributed systems — Google SRE Book

questions.scenario: Offline, a pairwise judge prefers prompt B over prompt A. In a two-week A/B test, B has a lower thumbs-up rate and a higher escalation-to-human rate than A, with a sample large enough to rule out noise.
questions.stem: What should the team do?
options: Retrain the judge to agree with the A/B result and rerun the offline eval
Keep A, examine B's escalated conversations, and add those failure cases to the eval set so offline results track real traffic
Average the offline and online results and ship whichever wins on the combined score
Ship B, because the offline judge is more objective than user behaviour
questions.explanation: Online metrics measure real user outcomes; offline evals measure only the cases in the set. When they disagree, the eval set is missing something, so the failing production conversations should become new tasks. This is how a golden set built from real traffic stays representative.
rationales: Tuning the judge to match one result without understanding the failures hides the gap rather than explaining it.
Correct. Trust the outcome data, diagnose the gap, and feed real failures back into the eval set.
Averaging incomparable metrics obscures the clear signal that B is worse for users.
The offline judge covers only the cases in the set and is subject to known biases; user outcomes reflect real traffic.

sources.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: An application calls a model through a moving alias. Quality complaints rise one morning with no deploy on the team's side, and the team later learns the alias now points to a newer model.
questions.stem: Which practice best prevents this?
options: Switch to a different provider's alias, which never changes
Rely on users to report problems and roll back afterwards
Keep the alias but lower the temperature to reduce behavioural drift
Pin a specific model snapshot ID and run the regression suite on any new snapshot before switching
questions.explanation: A model change is a product change. Pinning snapshot IDs makes upgrades deliberate (every Claude model ID is a pinned snapshot), and running the regression suite on the candidate before switching catches regressions before users do.
rationales: Aliases at any provider can move to new models; that is what an alias is for.
Waiting for complaints means users find the regression first.
Temperature does not prevent a model swap and is unsupported or ignored on many current models.
Correct. Pinned snapshots plus pre-switch evals turn silent model changes into reviewed ones.

sources.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: A team is turning a month of production conversations into the first eval set for a refund agent.
questions.stem: Which two practices should they follow? (Select two.)
options: Keep only tasks where two domain experts would agree on whether a result passes
Drop conversations the current system fails so the baseline starts near 100%
Replace real conversations with synthetic ones written by the team, so the set is cleaner
Include should-not-happen cases, such as requests where the agent must not issue a refund
questions.explanation: Anthropic's guidance is to test both what should and should not happen and to use unambiguous tasks that experts would grade the same way. Real failures are the most valuable starting tasks, so removing them or replacing real traffic with invented prompts defeats the purpose.
rationales: Correct. Unambiguous tasks make pass/fail meaningful and graders consistent.
Real failures are exactly the tasks the eval set should start from.
Synthetic prompts can supplement real traffic, but the set should be grounded in what users actually send.
Correct. Without should-not-happen cases, a system that over-acts looks perfect.

sources.title: Demystifying evals for AI agents — Anthropic Engineering

questions.scenario: A team uses a pairwise LLM judge to choose between two summarisation prompts. They want to reduce known judge biases before using the results to pick a winner.
questions.stem: Which two changes address documented judge biases? (Select two.)
options: Have the judge write its reasoning before the verdict and sample several judgments per pair
Use the same model family as one of the candidates, since it understands that style best
Evaluate every pair in both orders and aggregate, treating order-dependent verdicts as ties
Instruct the judge to prefer the more detailed summary when unsure
questions.explanation: Wang et al. propose Balanced Position Calibration (swap the order and aggregate) and Multiple Evidence Calibration (evidence before the score, several samples) to counter judge unfairness. Using the candidates' own model family invites self-preference, and favouring detail amplifies verbosity bias.
rationales: Correct. Evidence-first, multi-sample judging is Wang et al.'s Multiple Evidence Calibration.
LLM evaluators favour their own generations, so this introduces self-preference bias.
Correct. Swapping positions and aggregating counters position bias.
This builds verbosity bias into the rubric instead of controlling it.
